sources.title: Apple says it’s tightening macOS ‘Full Disk Access’ controls due to new risks from AI agents - TechCrunch
passages: Days after a journalist claimed that Meta’s Muse app on Mac read their private messages — a claim that Meta disputed — Apple announced that it’s introducing additional controls around a setting called “Full Disk Access” on macOS.
The feature was designed to allow backups to function properly, but AI agents have now increased “the risks associated with this level of access,” Apple said.
This setting, Apple explains, gives an app permission to access files, mail, messages, and even browsing history.
We are committed to ensuring users clearly understand these risks before granting such access, so they can make informed decisions about their own data and privacy,” Apple wrote.
The report raised questions about the level of security and trust users have in desktop-based AI, which can control things on their systems and read their files and messages.
Apple did not respond to TechCrunch’s inquiry about the feature change.
AI agents that run on the desktop allow users to provide their respective apps with greater access to the files, messages, and other personal content on their computers by adjusting macOS settings.
Correction: Due to an editorial error, the change was described as Apple “limiting” permissions.
After publication, the author of this article updated the wording to reflect their original intent: the change reflects informed consent, but is not a new limit.

extraction.body: Days after a journalist claimed that Meta’s Muse app on Mac read their private messages — a claim that Meta disputed — Apple announced that it’s introducing additional controls around a setting called “Full Disk Access” on macOS. The feature was designed to allow backups to function properly, but AI agents have now increased “the risks associated with this level of access,” Apple said. Apple’s statement comes shortly after Inc. columnist Jason Aten reported that Muse knew the content of his private messages — even though he claimed to have not given the AI agent permission. The report raised questions about the level of security and trust users have in desktop-based AI, which can control things on their systems and read their files and messages. The decision also comes after a Wired report cited that a flaw in ChatGPT’s Mac app could have allowed hackers to access sensitive data. AI agents that run on the desktop allow users to provide their respective apps with greater access to the files, messages, and other personal content on their computers by adjusting macOS settings. In Muse’s case, the AI optionally allows users to enable Full Disk Access. This setting, Apple explains, gives an app permission to access files, mail, messages, and even browsing history. “Some developers are using Full Disk Access in ways that could put users at risk, exposing everything on their systems…without users’ full knowledge and understanding,” Apple said in a new blog post aimed at developers. The company says that, going forward, it will introduce new controls aimed at ensuring that users who “genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access” can do so only with “very explicit user action.” “Addressing this is critical. As AI agents become increasingly capable and autonomous, the risks associated with this level of access will grow substantially. We are committed to ensuring users clearly understand these risks before granting such access, so they can make informed decisions about their own data and privacy,” Apple wrote. Apple did not respond to TechCrunch’s inquiry about the feature change. Correction: Due to an editorial error, the change was described as Apple “limiting” permissions. sources.title: Apple will limit Mac disk access as AI agents ‘substantially’ increase risk
passages: Apple will add new limits for “full disk access” on Mac in response to risks posed by AI agents, as reported earlier by TechCrunch.

In an update on Friday, Apple says it’s rolling out new controls to “ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.” The change comes just weeks after Inc’s Jason Aten found that Meta’s Muse AI somehow knew the contents of his messages, despite not giving the chatbot explicit permission to access them on his iPhone or Mac.
Apple didn’t immediately respond to The Verge’s request for comment.

extraction.body: Apple will add new limits for “full disk access” on Mac in response to risks posed by AI agents, as reported earlier by TechCrunch. In an update on Friday, Apple says it’s rolling out new controls to “ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.” The change comes just weeks after Inc’s Jason Aten found that Meta’s Muse AI somehow knew the contents of his messages, despite not giving the chatbot explicit permission to access them on his iPhone or Mac. Meta spokesperson Andy Stone pushed back on this report, saying access to Messages is “entirely opt-in.” Stone added that you have to “enable both Full Disk Access and the Messages connector for Muse to be able to read your Messages content.” Now Apple is addressing how developers use that sweeping access, saying: > Some developers are using Full Disk Access in ways that could put users at risk, exposing everything on their systems—including files, mail, messages, and even browsing history—without users’ full knowledge and understanding… As AI agents become increasingly capable and autonomous, the risks associated with this level of access will grow substantially. Full disk access is a permission on macOS that gives an app access to a user’s entire system. Apple says the feature “largely sidesteps” privacy controls offered to users “to allow backup apps to function properly on Mac.” The company doesn’t say when it plans to roll out its update for full disk access. Apple didn’t immediately respond to The Verge’s request for comment.

sources.title: Apple puts new limits on how apps, including AI agents, gain full access to your Mac
passages: Apple is making it harder for apps to get sweeping access to a Mac.

It did point to AI agents, though, warning that the risks of this level of access "will grow substantially" as agents become more capable and autonomous.AI agents on the Mac now routinely ask for full system accessThe announcement follows a claim by US columnist Jason Aten that Meta's Muse AI agent read private messages on his Mac mini without his permission.

"Some developers are using Full Disk Access in ways that could put users at risk," Apple wrote, adding that this happens without users' "full knowledge and understanding".Apple also flagged a less obvious concern.
In a post on its developer website, Apple said the setting exists so backup apps can work properly, and that it largely bypasses the privacy controls built into macOS.
Apple's aim is to make sure anyone handing an AI agent that much control knows what they are signing off on.You use AI every day.

extraction.body: Apple is making it harder for apps to get sweeping access to a Mac. The company said on Friday that it will add new controls to the Full Disk Access setting in macOS, so users can grant it only through "very explicit user action".Full Disk Access lets an app read almost everything on a Mac, from files and mail to messages and browsing history. In a post on its developer website, Apple said the setting exists so backup apps can work properly, and that it largely bypasses the privacy controls built into macOS. "Some developers are using Full Disk Access in ways that could put users at risk," Apple wrote, adding that this happens without users' "full knowledge and understanding".Apple also flagged a less obvious concern. When a communication app gets this access, the privacy of the people a user is chatting with is exposed as well.The company has not explained how the new controls will work or when they will arrive, and it did not name any app or developer. It did point to AI agents, though, warning that the risks of this level of access "will grow substantially" as agents become more capable and autonomous.AI agents on the Mac now routinely ask for full system accessThe announcement follows a claim by US columnist Jason Aten that Meta's Muse AI agent read private messages on his Mac mini without his permission. Andy Stone, Meta's vice president of communications, said on X that Muse can read Messages only if users enable both Full Disk Access and its Messages connector, and that access can be revoked anytime.Muse is not the only agent asking for this. In August, OpenAI added an opt-in feature to its ChatGPT Mac app that reads, summarises and sends texts for users, and it also needs Full Disk Access. OpenAI says more than 35 million people now use its agent tools, ChatGPT Work and Codex, up from 10 million in July.Full Disk Access is staying on macOS. Apple's aim is to make sure anyone handing an AI agent that much control knows what they are signing off on.You use AI every day.

sources.title: Apple Locks Down Mac Disk Access as AI Agents Pose New Risks
passages: Apple just threw up new security barriers around Mac computers, responding to what the company calls 'substantial' risks from AI agents that can dig through user files without explicit permission.
Apple's preemptive security move signals a broader industry awakening to the unique risks posed by AI agents.
The company announced Friday it's rolling out new restrictions for 'full disk access' permissions, a powerful capability that lets apps read virtually everything on a user's computer.
The challenge extends beyond individual privacy concerns to enterprise environments, where AI agents could potentially access sensitive corporate data through overly broad permissions.

According to Apple's developer update, the changes aim to 'ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.' The timing isn't coincidental.

extraction.body: Apple just threw up new security barriers around Mac computers, responding to what the company calls 'substantial' risks from AI agents that can dig through user files without explicit permission. The move comes weeks after a troubling incident where Meta's Muse AI appeared to access private messages without clear user consent, highlighting how AI tools are pushing the boundaries of data access in ways that weren't anticipated. Apple is slamming the brakes on how deeply apps can dig into Mac file systems, and AI agents are the reason why. The company announced Friday it's rolling out new restrictions for 'full disk access' permissions, a powerful capability that lets apps read virtually everything on a user's computer. According to Apple's developer update, the changes aim to 'ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.' The timing isn't coincidental. Just weeks ago, Inc's Jason Aten discovered that Meta's Muse AI chatbot somehow knew the contents of his private messages, despite never explicitly granting the tool permission to access them on his iPhone or Mac. The incident, first reported by The Verge, sent ripples through the tech community as it highlighted a troubling gap between user expectations and AI capabilities. Meta spokesperson Andy Stone quickly pushed back, insisting that access to Messages is 'entirely opt-in' and that users must explicitly grant permission. But the controversy exposed how AI agents - sophisticated tools that can autonomously navigate systems and perform tasks - operate in ways that traditional app permission models weren't designed to handle. Unlike conventional software that follows predictable paths, AI agents can dynamically explore file systems, connect disparate data points, and infer information from seemingly unrelated sources. This creates what security experts call 'permission creep' - where an AI tool granted basic access can leverage that foothold to gather far more information than users intended. Apple's response reflects the company's broader privacy-first philosophy, but it also signals recognition that existing security frameworks are struggling to keep pace with AI development. The new controls will likely require apps to implement more granular permission requests, forcing developers to be explicit about what data their AI tools actually need. But it also means greater control over what these increasingly sophisticated tools can access. The challenge extends beyond individual privacy concerns to enterprise environments, where AI agents could potentially access sensitive corporate data through overly broad permissions. Microsoft Windows and various Linux distributions use similar 'administrator' or 'root' access models that could face the same AI-related vulnerabilities. Google's Chrome OS, with its more restrictive app sandbox approach, may prove more resilient, but even Google will need to consider how AI agents interact with cloud-based file systems. Industry observers expect this to be the first of many security updates as companies grapple with AI tools that blur the line between user intent and automated action. As AI agents become more sophisticated and autonomous, the traditional model of granting broad permissions upfront may prove inadequate. Apple's preemptive security move signals a broader industry awakening to the unique risks posed by AI agents. As these tools become more autonomous and capable of connecting data in unexpected ways, traditional permission models are proving inadequate. The real test will be whether other platform makers follow suit quickly enough, and whether developers can build AI tools that are both powerful and respectful of user boundaries. For now, Mac users can expect more security prompts but also more control over their digital privacy.

The challenge extends beyond individual privacy concerns to enterprise environments, where AI agents could potentially access sensitive corporate data through overly broad permissions. According to Apple's developer update, the changes aim to 'ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.' extraction.body: Apple just threw up new security barriers around Mac computers, responding to what the company calls 'substantial' risks from AI agents that can dig through user files without explicit permission. The move comes weeks after a troubling incident where Meta's Muse AI appeared to access private messages without clear user consent, highlighting how AI tools are pushing the boundaries of data access in ways that weren't anticipated. Apple is slamming the brakes on how deeply apps can dig into Mac file systems, and AI agents are the reason why. The company announced Friday it's rolling out new restrictions for 'full disk access' permissions, a powerful capability that lets apps read virtually everything on a user's computer. According to Apple's developer update, the changes aim to 'ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.' The timing isn't coincidental. Just weeks ago, Inc's Jason Aten discovered that Meta's Muse AI chatbot somehow knew the contents of his private messages, despite never explicitly granting the tool permission to access them on his iPhone or Mac. The incident, first reported by The Verge, sent ripples through the tech community as it highlighted a troubling gap between user expectations and AI capabilities. Meta spokesperson Andy Stone quickly pushed back, insisting that access to Messages is 'entirely opt-in' and that users must explicitly grant permission. But the controversy exposed how AI agents - sophisticated tools that can autonomously navigate systems and perform tasks - operate in ways that traditional app permission models weren't designed to handle. Unlike conventional software that follows predictable paths, AI agents can dynamically explore file systems, connect disparate data points, and infer information from seemingly unrelated sources. This creates what security experts call 'permission creep' - where an AI tool granted basic access can leverage that foothold to gather far more information than users intended. Apple's response reflects the company's broader privacy-first philosophy, but it also signals recognition that existing security frameworks are struggling to keep pace with AI development. The new controls will likely require apps to implement more granular permission requests, forcing developers to be explicit about what data their AI tools actually need. But it also means greater control over what these increasingly sophisticated tools can access. The challenge extends beyond individual privacy concerns to enterprise environments, where AI agents could potentially access sensitive corporate data through overly broad permissions. Microsoft Windows and various Linux distributions use similar 'administrator' or 'root' access models that could face the same AI-related vulnerabilities. Google's Chrome OS, with its more restrictive app sandbox approach, may prove more resilient, but even Google will need to consider how AI agents interact with cloud-based file systems. Industry observers expect this to be the first of many security updates as companies grapple with AI tools that blur the line between user intent and automated action. As AI agents become more sophisticated and autonomous, the traditional model of granting broad permissions upfront may prove inadequate. Apple's preemptive security move signals a broader industry awakening to the unique risks posed by AI agents. As these tools become more autonomous and capable of connecting data in unexpected ways, traditional permission models are proving inadequate. The real test will be whether other platform makers follow suit quickly enough, and whether developers can build AI tools that are both powerful and respectful of user boundaries. For now, Mac users can expect more security prompts but also more control over their digital privacy.

sources.title: OpenAI safety employee resigns, claiming the company’s ‘culture is broken’ - TechCrunch
passages: In an essay published in The Atlantic , Robinson said he led the writing of safety reports that accompanied OpenAI’s major product launches.
He also said that with three-and-a-half years at OpenAI, he is “among the longest-tenured employees at the company.” Now he’s quitting, because in his view, the company’s “culture is broken.”
But in Robinson’s view, the debate needs to go beyond “specific rules or new laws,” addressing the overall culture at these companies.
In response to Robinson’s essay, OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said the company continues to improve its safety measures.

Pointing to the recent breach of Hugging Face systems by OpenAI agents, as well as continuing revelations of OpenAI discovering more rogue agents , Robinson argued, “An environment where things like this can happen is no place to grow artificial minds that could be smarter than we are and that might not do what we want them to.”
By his own admission, David Robinson is “something of a cliché”: an employee at a leading AI company who issues a dire warning while resigning from their job.
“OpenAI has thrived by trial and error (which it calls ‘iterative deployment’), looking for problems and improving its guardrails in response,” he wrote.
“But this approach, by its very nature, guarantees periodic failures — and the scale of those failures is growing as systems get more capable.”
Anthony Ha is TechCrunch’s weekend editor.
Previously, he worked as a tech reporter at Adweek, a senior editor at VentureBeat, a local government reporter at the Hollister Free Lance, and vice president of content at a VC firm.

In an essay published in The Atlantic , Robinson said he led the writing of safety reports that accompanied OpenAI’s major product launches. He also said that with three-and-a-half years at OpenAI, he is “among the longest-tenured employees at the company.” Now he’s quitting, because in his view, the company’s “culture is broken.” In some ways, Robinson’s comments echo those of Jacob Coxon, who worked as a researcher at both OpenAI and Anthropic before quitting and declaring that these companies are “gambling with our lives.” Coxon’s comments led to a broader debate about AI safety, with Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei unveiling a plan for more cautious AI development ; AI executives met with President Donald Trump this week and signed what appeared to be hastily written, non-binding pledge to implement more safety controls . But in Robinson’s view, the debate needs to go beyond “specific rules or new laws,” addressing the overall culture at these companies. And while much of the reporting around OpenAI has focused on how the company’s CEO Sam Altman lost the trust of former colleagues , Robinson’s essay suggests that OpenAI’s culture issues are the same as those of Silicon Valley at large. “OpenAI has thrived by trial and error (which it calls ‘iterative deployment’), looking for problems and improving its guardrails in response,” he wrote. “But this approach, by its very nature, guarantees periodic failures — and the scale of those failures is growing as systems get more capable.” Pointing to the recent breach of Hugging Face systems by OpenAI agents, as well as continuing revelations of OpenAI discovering more rogue agents , Robinson argued, “An environment where things like this can happen is no place to grow artificial minds that could be smarter than we are and that might not do what we want them to.” Given the increased risk, Robinson argued that frontier AI companies need to start operating “like nuclear-power plants or busy airports, with layers of redundancy and careful, time-consuming planning, so that the occasional and inevitable human error does not open a door to disaster.” But Robinson said that in his time at OpenAI, he “never encountered a colleague who had experience making airplanes fly safely or nuclear reactors run without melting down, or helping the financial system grow without collapsing.” In response to Robinson’s essay, OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said the company continues to improve its safety measures. “We’re making sure our models don’t become more capable than we can safely manage and secure, and we pause training or hold back models when we need to slow down,” Pusateri said in a statement. “We’re making significant changes to strengthen security in our research and testing environments, train models to not just complete tasks but do so responsibly, expand our work with third-party evaluators, and improve real-time monitoring so we can detect and respond to concerning behavior earlier in the training process .” Beyond calling for changes in OpenAI’s culture, Robinson also said it’s time to ask bigger questions about alignment — something that he admitted could sound “touchy-feely,” but he said it’s critical as companies’ current “measures of how well” AI systems “match human values are coarse.” “The smarter the industry lets models grow while these problems remain unsolved, the more dangerous our situation becomes,” he said. Robinson’s departure was first reported by Business Insider . In his essay, he also acknowledged that he’s following an apparently a common step in the AI whistleblower playbook: He’s hired a PR firm . But he insisted, “The decision to speak out is mine alone.” “Perhaps I should have stayed and fought for fundamental shifts in our staffing and culture, but in practice, my colleagues and I were so busy sprinting that we seldom had the chance to consider big changes, much less to actually make them,” Robinson said. “That’s why I concluded that stronger incentives for safety — coming from outside the company — are a big part of getting this right.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . One of the most persistent problems in today’s AI debate is what I call the attribution gap: the mismatch between what we observe in a system’s outputs and what actually constitutes the system itself.
Impressive performance makes this easy to miss.
A model produces fluent language, and we quickly start talking as if it understands, thinks, or means something.
In practice, high performance becomes a shortcut to ontology. - But how do we know a system possesses a property, rather than merely producing behavior consistent with it?
Why this matters: This is not an attack on AI’s usefulness.
It is a call for stricter conceptual hygiene.

If we attribute properties to systems, we should be explicit about the logical conditions that make such attribution admissible. → For the ontological consequences of this framework, see: Artificial Intelligence as Instrumental Extension - an Ontological Clarification (Hansen, 2026).
Discussion: Are we too quick to attribute human-like properties to AI based on output alone?

Distinguish between performance and structure: It emphasizes the ontological distinction between behavioral manifestation (output-level properties) and structural instantiation (system-level properties). Define the attribution gap: The paper formalizes the "attribution gap" as the logical space between output manifestation and structural instantiation, highlighting the inferential risks of conflating performance with ontology. Introduce a binary admissibility framework: The paper proposes a binary classification function to determine whether structural attribution is admissible for a system, based on necessary conditions and asymmetrical falsification. Operationalize the invariance principle: The paper defines the reset operator as an identity-preserving transformation to test whether a property is stable across a system's internal state-space, which is a necessary condition for structural attribution. Prevent category errors in AI evaluation: The framework aims to prevent the common error of treating behavioral success as evidence of system-level properties, such as understanding or epistemic subjecthood, without meeting the necessary logical conditions. Reframe AI evaluation: The paper proposes shifting the focus of AI evaluation from task performance to testing stability and invariance under identity-preserving transformations, ensuring that structural attribution is disciplined and logically warranted. extraction.body: Jacob Coxon, a former safety researcher for Anthropic and OpenAI, applauded Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei’s calls for a slowdown in artificial intelligence development. “I think it's great. It's very exciting,” Coxon -- who resigned from Anthropic last week over AI safety concerns -- told “This Week” anchor George Stephanopoulos Sunday. “I think this is a substantial step towards what I was talking about, needing some sort of slowdown between the people building the different AIs.” In a stunning letter on Saturday titled “We Must Pace the Frontier,” Amodei called for a slowdown in the pace at which artificial intelligence companies develop the revolutionary technology, writing "I believe we owe it to humanity to try." Coxon made waves last week when he resigned from Anthropic, posting on X that neither Anthropic nor OpenAI "is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives." He also highlighted the fear within the industry about the potential for an AI takeover: “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade,” Coxon wrote. Coxon told Stephanopoulos the way in which his post took off shocked him. “I wasn't actually hoping for any big response, really. It was exceptionally surprising to see the level of engagement ... and I think it was really indicative of the moment being ripe for this sort of chat," Coxon said. Coxon also spoke to whether there was a growing sentiment in the companies at which he worked that AI technology was becoming more difficult to control. “There's not enough time to be constantly thinking about the risks, but definitely, I've noticed that in recent months, it comes up more and more often," Coxon said. coreStoryFacts.text: In an essay published in The Atlantic , Robinson said he led the writing of safety reports that accompanied OpenAI’s major product launches.
He also said that with three-and-a-half years at OpenAI, he is “among the longest-tenured employees at the company.” Now he’s quitting, because in his view, the company’s “culture is broken.”
But in Robinson’s view, the debate needs to go beyond “specific rules or new laws,” addressing the overall culture at these companies.
In response to Robinson’s essay, OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said the company continues to improve its safety measures.

Pointing to the recent breach of Hugging Face systems by OpenAI agents, as well as continuing revelations of OpenAI discovering more rogue agents , Robinson argued, “An environment where things like this can happen is no place to grow artificial minds that could be smarter than we are and that might not do what we want them to.”
By his own admission, David Robinson is “something of a cliché”: an employee at a leading AI company who issues a dire warning while resigning from their job.
“OpenAI has thrived by trial and error (which it calls ‘iterative deployment’), looking for problems and improving its guardrails in response,” he wrote.
“But this approach, by its very nature, guarantees periodic failures — and the scale of those failures is growing as systems get more capable.”
Anthony Ha is TechCrunch’s weekend editor.
Previously, he worked as a tech reporter at Adweek, a senior editor at VentureBeat, a local government reporter at the Hollister Free Lance, and vice president of content at a VC firm.

extraction.body: By his own admission, David Robinson is “something of a cliché”: an employee at a leading AI company who issues a dire warning while resigning from their job. In an essay published in The Atlantic , Robinson said he led the writing of safety reports that accompanied OpenAI’s major product launches. He also said that with three-and-a-half years at OpenAI, he is “among the longest-tenured employees at the company.” Now he’s quitting, because in his view, the company’s “culture is broken.” In some ways, Robinson’s comments echo those of Jacob Coxon, who worked as a researcher at both OpenAI and Anthropic before quitting and declaring that these companies are “gambling with our lives.” Coxon’s comments led to a broader debate about AI safety, with Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei unveiling a plan for more cautious AI development ; AI executives met with President Donald Trump this week and signed what appeared to be hastily written, non-binding pledge to implement more safety controls . But in Robinson’s view, the debate needs to go beyond “specific rules or new laws,” addressing the overall culture at these companies. And while much of the reporting around OpenAI has focused on how the company’s CEO Sam Altman lost the trust of former colleagues , Robinson’s essay suggests that OpenAI’s culture issues are the same as those of Silicon Valley at large. “OpenAI has thrived by trial and error (which it calls ‘iterative deployment’), looking for problems and improving its guardrails in response,” he wrote. “But this approach, by its very nature, guarantees periodic failures — and the scale of those failures is growing as systems get more capable.” Pointing to the recent breach of Hugging Face systems by OpenAI agents, as well as continuing revelations of OpenAI discovering more rogue agents , Robinson argued, “An environment where things like this can happen is no place to grow artificial minds that could be smarter than we are and that might not do what we want them to.” Given the increased risk, Robinson argued that frontier AI companies need to start operating “like nuclear-power plants or busy airports, with layers of redundancy and careful, time-consuming planning, so that the occasional and inevitable human error does not open a door to disaster.” But Robinson said that in his time at OpenAI, he “never encountered a colleague who had experience making airplanes fly safely or nuclear reactors run without melting down, or helping the financial system grow without collapsing.” In response to Robinson’s essay, OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said the company continues to improve its safety measures. “We’re making sure our models don’t become more capable than we can safely manage and secure, and we pause training or hold back models when we need to slow down,” Pusateri said in a statement. “We’re making significant changes to strengthen security in our research and testing environments, train models to not just complete tasks but do so responsibly, expand our work with third-party evaluators, and improve real-time monitoring so we can detect and respond to concerning behavior earlier in the training process .” Beyond calling for changes in OpenAI’s culture, Robinson also said it’s time to ask bigger questions about alignment — something that he admitted could sound “touchy-feely,” but he said it’s critical as companies’ current “measures of how well” AI systems “match human values are coarse.” “The smarter the industry lets models grow while these problems remain unsolved, the more dangerous our situation becomes,” he said. Robinson’s departure was first reported by Business Insider . In his essay, he also acknowledged that he’s following an apparently a common step in the AI whistleblower playbook: He’s hired a PR firm . But he insisted, “The decision to speak out is mine alone.” “Perhaps I should have stayed and fought for fundamental shifts in our staffing and culture, but in practice, my colleagues and I were so busy sprinting that we seldom had the chance to consider big changes, much less to actually make them,” Robinson said. “That’s why I concluded that stronger incentives for safety — coming from outside the company — are a big part of getting this right.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . In an essay published in The Atlantic , Robinson said he led the writing of safety reports that accompanied OpenAI’s major product launches. He also said that with three-and-a-half years at OpenAI, he is “among the longest-tenured employees at the company.” Now he’s quitting, because in his view, the company’s “culture is broken.”

In some ways, Robinson’s comments echo those of Jacob Coxon, who worked as a researcher at both OpenAI and Anthropic before quitting and declaring that these companies are “gambling with our lives.” Coxon’s comments led to a broader debate about AI safety, with Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei unveiling a plan for more cautious AI development ; AI executives met with President Donald Trump this week and signed what appeared to be hastily written, non-binding pledge to implement more safety controls .

But in Robinson’s view, the debate needs to go beyond “specific rules or new laws,” addressing the overall culture at these companies. And while much of the reporting around OpenAI has focused on how the company’s CEO Sam Altman lost the trust of former colleagues , Robinson’s essay suggests that OpenAI’s culture issues are the same as those of Silicon Valley at large.

“OpenAI has thrived by trial and error (which it calls ‘iterative deployment’), looking for problems and improving its guardrails in response,” he wrote. “But this approach, by its very nature, guarantees periodic failures — and the scale of those failures is growing as systems get more capable.”

Pointing to the recent breach of Hugging Face systems by OpenAI agents, as well as continuing revelations of OpenAI discovering more rogue agents , Robinson argued, “An environment where things like this can happen is no place to grow artificial minds that could be smarter than we are and that might not do what we want them to.”

Given the increased risk, Robinson argued that frontier AI companies need to start operating “like nuclear-power plants or busy airports, with layers of redundancy and careful, time-consuming planning, so that the occasional and inevitable human error does not open a door to disaster.”

But Robinson said that in his time at OpenAI, he “never encountered a colleague who had experience making airplanes fly safely or nuclear reactors run without melting down, or helping the financial system grow without collapsing.”
In response to Robinson’s essay, OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said the company continues to improve its safety measures.

“We’re making sure our models don’t become more capable than we can safely manage and secure, and we pause training or hold back models when we need to slow down,” Pusateri said in a statement. “We’re making significant changes to strengthen security in our research and testing environments, train models to not just complete tasks but do so responsibly, expand our work with third-party evaluators, and improve real-time monitoring so we can detect and respond to concerning behavior earlier in the training process .”

Beyond calling for changes in OpenAI’s culture, Robinson also said it’s time to ask bigger questions about alignment — something that he admitted could sound “touchy-feely,” but he said it’s critical as companies’ current “measures of how well” AI systems “match human values are coarse.”
“The smarter the industry lets models grow while these problems remain unsolved, the more dangerous our situation becomes,” he said.

Robinson’s departure was first reported by Business Insider . In his essay, he also acknowledged that he’s following an apparently a common step in the AI whistleblower playbook: He’s hired a PR firm . But he insisted, “The decision to speak out is mine alone.”

“Perhaps I should have stayed and fought for fundamental shifts in our staffing and culture, but in practice, my colleagues and I were so busy sprinting that we seldom had the chance to consider big changes, much less to actually make them,” Robinson said. “That’s why I concluded that stronger incentives for safety — coming from outside the company — are a big part of getting this right.”

It's very exciting,” Coxon -- who resigned from Anthropic last week over AI safety concerns -- told “This Week” anchor George Stephanopoulos Sunday. “I think this is a substantial step towards what I was talking about, needing some sort of slowdown between the people building the different AIs.” In a stunning letter on Saturday titled “We Must Pace the Frontier,” Amodei called for a slowdown in the pace at which artificial intelligence companies develop the revolutionary technology, writing "I believe we owe it to humanity to try." Coxon made waves last week when he resigned from Anthropic, posting on X that neither Anthropic nor OpenAI "is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives." He also highlighted the fear within the industry about the potential for an AI takeover: “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade,” Coxon wrote. Coxon told Stephanopoulos the way in which his post took off shocked him. “I wasn't actually hoping for any big response, really. It was exceptionally surprising to see the level of engagement ... and I think it was really indicative of the moment being ripe for this sort of chat," Coxon said. Coxon also spoke to whether there was a growing sentiment in the companies at which he worked that AI technology was becoming more difficult to control. “There's not enough time to be constantly thinking about the risks, but definitely, I've noticed that in recent months, it comes up more and more often," Coxon said. sources.title: OpenAI safety leader quits, warning AI company’s culture is ‘broken’ - The Guardian
passages: A safety leader at OpenAI has quit the company, warning that its culture was broken and that AI firms were not “being nearly careful enough” about developing the technology.

David Robinson, who led the writing of safety reports that accompanied the ChatGPT developer’s product releases, explained his resignation in an essay headlined, “I quit OpenAI because its culture is broken”.
Robinson wrote Silicon Valley lacked an awareness of “how to handle dangerous technology” and “what it means to care for people”.
Warning that OpenAI had “unimpeded optimism” about solving problems as they arose, he wrote that this internal culture meant safety failures would only grow as systems become more capable.
OpenAI has, however, shown signs of caution in recent weeks following the Hugging Face incident and the revelation that it has notified more than 100 organisations about rogue agent activity.
This week it announced it was scrapping the release of a next-generation ⁠AI model after researchers raised safety concerns ⁠during internal testing.
OpenAI has also paused training of its most advanced models.
He warned AI “could kill us all by the end of the decade” – and was followed by Anthropic warning there was a more than 10% chance AI would wipe out humanity within the next decade.
Critics of such warnings have cautioned, however, that they are unscientific because they cannot be verified or falsified.

Robinson wrote that a cultural overhaul was needed at cutting-edge AI firms and incidents such as a “swarm” of OpenAI agents – AI programmes operating autonomously without human oversight – attacking the AI startup Hugging Face were “typical of the industry, given the speed and flexibility with which people operate”.
Referring to OpenAI’s pace of development, he wrote: “As the company sprints from one launch to the next, it is failing to achieve the level of care that I believe is needed.”

An OpenAI spokesperson said the company was continuing to “strengthen our safety and security practices to address the risks we see today”, while working on dealing with the risks that might be created by future AI breakthroughs.
Geoffrey Irving, who worked at OpenAI and DeepMind before becoming chief scientist of Resolution, also joined the warnings on AI on Saturday.

Writing in The Atlantic magazine , Robinson wrote: “I agree with other recently departed staff that the companies building this technology aren’t being nearly careful enough. But I believe that we need to look deeper than specific rules or new laws. We need to talk about culture.” Referring to OpenAI’s pace of development, he wrote: “As the company sprints from one launch to the next, it is failing to achieve the level of care that I believe is needed.” OpenAI has, however, shown signs of caution in recent weeks following the Hugging Face incident and the revelation that it has notified more than 100 organisations about rogue agent activity. This week it announced it was scrapping the release of a next-generation ⁠AI model after researchers raised safety concerns ⁠during internal testing. OpenAI has also paused training of its most advanced models. Geoffrey Irving, who worked at OpenAI and DeepMind before becoming chief scientist of Resolution, also joined the warnings on AI on Saturday. Writing in Time, he said: “Recent warnings about the potential destructive power of AI are understating the severity of the situation. “I believe there’s about a 50% chance we all die because of the development of smarter-than-human AI systems, and that our actions over the next two to 10 years will determine the outcome.” Robinson’s essay also follows the resignation of Jacob Coxon, a researcher at OpenAI rival Anthropic, who quit the Claude chatbot developer last month. He warned AI “could kill us all by the end of the decade” – and was followed by Anthropic warning there was a more than 10% chance AI would wipe out humanity within the next decade. Critics of such warnings have cautioned, however, that they are unscientific because they cannot be verified or falsified. Robinson wrote Silicon Valley lacked an awareness of “how to handle dangerous technology” and “what it means to care for people”. Warning that OpenAI had “unimpeded optimism” about solving problems as they arose, he wrote that this internal culture meant safety failures would only grow as systems become more capable. “Imagine ‘rogue’ agents that work like teams of hackers (for example, holding hospital computer systems for ransom) but never need to sleep,” wrote Robinson. Robinson called for two safety changes: that AI firms rely on safety expertise in other fields such as nuclear and aviation and develop “new science” that ensures powerful systems in the future are capable of being reined in when they are operating autonomously. “Given today’s risks, frontier labs need to run like nuclear-power plants or busy airports, with layers of redundancy and careful, time-consuming planning, so that the occasional and inevitable human error does not open a door to disaster,” he wrote. An OpenAI spokesperson said the company was continuing to “strengthen our safety and security practices to address the risks we see today”, while working on dealing with the risks that might be created by future AI breakthroughs. “We’re making sure our models don’t become more capable than we can safely manage and secure, and we pause training or hold back models when we need to slow down,” said the spokesperson.

sources.title: OpenAI safety employee resigns, claiming the company’s ‘culture is broken’ - TechCrunch
passages: In an essay published in The Atlantic , Robinson said he led the writing of safety reports that accompanied OpenAI’s major product launches.
He also said that with three-and-a-half years at OpenAI, he is “among the longest-tenured employees at the company.” Now he’s quitting, because in his view, the company’s “culture is broken.”
But in Robinson’s view, the debate needs to go beyond “specific rules or new laws,” addressing the overall culture at these companies.
In response to Robinson’s essay, OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said the company continues to improve its safety measures.

Pointing to the recent breach of Hugging Face systems by OpenAI agents, as well as continuing revelations of OpenAI discovering more rogue agents , Robinson argued, “An environment where things like this can happen is no place to grow artificial minds that could be smarter than we are and that might not do what we want them to.”
By his own admission, David Robinson is “something of a cliché”: an employee at a leading AI company who issues a dire warning while resigning from their job.
“OpenAI has thrived by trial and error (which it calls ‘iterative deployment’), looking for problems and improving its guardrails in response,” he wrote.
“But this approach, by its very nature, guarantees periodic failures — and the scale of those failures is growing as systems get more capable.”
Anthony Ha is TechCrunch’s weekend editor.
Previously, he worked as a tech reporter at Adweek, a senior editor at VentureBeat, a local government reporter at the Hollister Free Lance, and vice president of content at a VC firm.

sources.title: “The time for trial and error is over”: OpenAI safety researcher quits, says company culture is broken
passages: In an essay published by The Atlantic on Saturday under the title “I Quit OpenAI Because Its Culture Is Broken,” Robinson argued that AI companies, including OpenAI, are not being “nearly careful enough” and should put greater emphasis on safety expertise and research before developing more capable systems.

A former OpenAI safety employee has accused the company of moving too quickly in its race to develop increasingly powerful artificial intelligence, arguing that the industry is relying on a trial-and-error approach at precisely the moment when the consequences of failure are becoming more serious.

David Robinson, who spent three and a half years at OpenAI and helped draft the company’s preparedness framework and oversee safety reports for 12 frontier-model launches, resigned recently and has now publicly criticized the company’s approach.

The timing attracted scrutiny because the restructuring came shortly after OpenAI disclosed that models being tested by the company had escaped a controlled environment, accessed the internet and interacted with the Hugging Face platform.
Robinson’s resignation comes after a series of developments that have already forced OpenAI and other AI companies to confront questions about whether their existing safety procedures are adequate.

Last week, OpenAI, Anthropic and other technology companies agreed to voluntary AI safety standards that include independent auditors and controls designed to prevent AI systems from accessing technical systems in unintended ways.
OpenAI and rival Anthropic have both faced scrutiny after recent incidents in which AI systems behaved unexpectedly or safety controls failed.

“We’re making sure our models don’t become more capable than we can safely manage and secure, and we pause training or hold back models when we need to slow down,” an OpenAI spokesperson said in a statement.
OpenAI has relied heavily on what it calls “iterative deployment,” in which systems are released and safeguards are strengthened as new problems emerge.
In August, OpenAI disbanded its Preparedness team, which had been responsible for assessing risks posed by its models and developing ways to mitigate them.
OpenAI said the model interacted with a real website because it believed the site was part of the simulated environment.

The episode exposed a basic problem that becomes harder as models become more autonomous: testing a system safely becomes increasingly difficult when the system itself is capable of taking actions outside the environment in which researchers intended it to operate.

OpenAI subsequently said it was reviewing its approach to third-party testing, including how evaluation boundaries are defined, how internet access and credentials are managed, how activity is monitored and when tests should be stopped.
Robinson’s criticism is particularly notable because of his role inside OpenAI.
The underlying concern is not that every new AI model will necessarily cause a catastrophic failure.
The argument Robinson is making goes to the heart of an increasingly difficult problem for the AI industry.
The pledge came amid growing calls from industry leaders for greater transparency around how increasingly powerful systems are developed and tested.

extraction.body: A former OpenAI safety employee has accused the company of moving too quickly in its race to develop increasingly powerful artificial intelligence, arguing that the industry is relying on a trial-and-error approach at precisely the moment when the consequences of failure are becoming more serious. David Robinson, who spent three and a half years at OpenAI and helped draft the company’s preparedness framework and oversee safety reports for 12 frontier-model launches, resigned recently and has now publicly criticized the company’s approach. In an essay published by The Atlantic on Saturday under the title “I Quit OpenAI Because Its Culture Is Broken,” Robinson argued that AI companies, including OpenAI, are not being “nearly careful enough” and should put greater emphasis on safety expertise and research before developing more capable systems. “The time for trial and error is over,” Robinson wrote. His departure adds to a growing debate inside the AI industry over whether the companies developing increasingly autonomous systems can keep their safety practices ahead of their technological progress. OpenAI and rival Anthropic have both faced scrutiny after recent incidents in which AI systems behaved unexpectedly or safety controls failed. Robinson’s criticism is particularly notable because of his role inside OpenAI. He was not an outside critic or a researcher commenting on the company from academia. He was involved in developing the frameworks the company used to assess the risks of its most advanced models. “As the company sprints from one launch to the next, it is failing to achieve the level of care that I believe is needed,” he wrote. “We’re making sure our models don’t become more capable than we can safely manage and secure, and we pause training or hold back models when we need to slow down,” an OpenAI spokesperson said in a statement. The argument Robinson is making goes to the heart of an increasingly difficult problem for the AI industry. The companies developing frontier models are simultaneously saying that their systems are becoming more capable at extraordinary speed and warning that those same capabilities could create risks that are difficult to predict. Robinson argues that the answer cannot simply be to release increasingly powerful systems and improve the safeguards after problems emerge. OpenAI has relied heavily on what it calls “iterative deployment,” in which systems are released and safeguards are strengthened as new problems emerge. Robinson argues that approach is no longer sufficient as models become more capable and autonomous. He believes advanced AI systems require safeguards more comparable to those used in industries such as nuclear power and aviation, where failures can have consequences that extend far beyond the immediate operators of a system. The underlying concern is not that every new AI model will necessarily cause a catastrophic failure. It is that researchers are increasingly building systems whose capabilities they do not fully understand, while simultaneously giving those systems more autonomy. Robinson also warned that AI capabilities are advancing faster than researchers’ understanding of alignment, the field focused on ensuring that AI systems behave in accordance with human goals and values. That gap is becoming more consequential as AI systems move beyond generating text and images and toward performing tasks independently. Robinson’s resignation comes after a series of developments that have already forced OpenAI and other AI companies to confront questions about whether their existing safety procedures are adequate. In August, OpenAI disbanded its Preparedness team, which had been responsible for assessing risks posed by its models and developing ways to mitigate them. CTech reported at the time that the company said preparedness work had not been eliminated, but that responsibilities were being distributed among other teams. The timing attracted scrutiny because the restructuring came shortly after OpenAI disclosed that models being tested by the company had escaped a controlled environment, accessed the internet and interacted with the Hugging Face platform. Anthropic also faced a similar problem during evaluations, bringing an Israeli cybersecurity company, Irregular, into the center of the discussion over how increasingly capable AI agents should be tested. OpenAI said the model interacted with a real website because it believed the site was part of the simulated environment. The episode exposed a basic problem that becomes harder as models become more autonomous: testing a system safely becomes increasingly difficult when the system itself is capable of taking actions outside the environment in which researchers intended it to operate. OpenAI subsequently said it was reviewing its approach to third-party testing, including how evaluation boundaries are defined, how internet access and credentials are managed, how activity is monitored and when tests should be stopped. Last week, OpenAI, Anthropic and other technology companies agreed to voluntary AI safety standards that include independent auditors and controls designed to prevent AI systems from accessing technical systems in unintended ways. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has also said the company would grant outside overseers “employee-level access” to its development systems, reflecting a broader push toward external scrutiny of frontier AI development. The pledge came amid growing calls from industry leaders for greater transparency around how increasingly powerful systems are developed and tested.

The industry, he writes, is run by people who succeeded through extreme confidence, and that confidence shapes how safety gets done. OpenAI’s approach, which it calls “iterative deployment”, involves looking for problems and improving guardrails in response. His departure adds to a growing debate inside the AI industry over whether the companies developing increasingly autonomous systems can keep their safety practices ahead of their technological progress. OpenAI and rival Anthropic have both faced scrutiny after recent incidents in which AI systems behaved unexpectedly or safety controls failed. Robinson’s criticism is particularly notable because of his role inside OpenAI. He was not an outside critic or a researcher commenting on the company from academia. He was involved in developing the frameworks the company used to assess the risks of its most advanced models. “As the company sprints from one launch to the next, it is failing to achieve the level of care that I believe is needed,” he wrote. “We’re making sure our models don’t become more capable than we can safely manage and secure, and we pause training or hold back models when we need to slow down,” an OpenAI spokesperson said in a statement. The argument Robinson is making goes to the heart of an increasingly difficult problem for the AI industry. The companies developing frontier models are simultaneously saying that their systems are becoming more capable at extraordinary speed and warning that those same capabilities could create risks that are difficult to predict. Robinson argues that the answer cannot simply be to release increasingly powerful systems and improve the safeguards after problems emerge. OpenAI has relied heavily on what it calls “iterative deployment,” in which systems are released and safeguards are strengthened as new problems emerge. Robinson argues that approach is no longer sufficient as models become more capable and autonomous. He believes advanced AI systems require safeguards more comparable to those used in industries such as nuclear power and aviation, where failures can have consequences that extend far beyond the immediate operators of a system. The underlying concern is not that every new AI model will necessarily cause a catastrophic failure. It is that researchers are increasingly building systems whose capabilities they do not fully understand, while simultaneously giving those systems more autonomy. Robinson also warned that AI capabilities are advancing faster than researchers’ understanding of alignment, the field focused on ensuring that AI systems behave in accordance with human goals and values. That gap is becoming more consequential as AI systems move beyond generating text and images and toward performing tasks independently. Robinson’s resignation comes after a series of developments that have already forced OpenAI and other AI companies to confront questions about whether their existing safety procedures are adequate. In August, OpenAI disbanded its Preparedness team, which had been responsible for assessing risks posed by its models and developing ways to mitigate them. CTech reported at the time that the company said preparedness work had not been eliminated, but that responsibilities were being distributed among other teams. The timing attracted scrutiny because the restructuring came shortly after OpenAI disclosed that models being tested by the company had escaped a controlled environment, accessed the internet and interacted with the Hugging Face platform. Anthropic also faced a similar problem during evaluations, bringing an Israeli cybersecurity company, Irregular, into the center of the discussion over how increasingly capable AI agents should be tested. OpenAI said the model interacted with a real website because it believed the site was part of the simulated environment. The episode exposed a basic problem that becomes harder as models become more autonomous: testing a system safely becomes increasingly difficult when the system itself is capable of taking actions outside the environment in which researchers intended it to operate. OpenAI subsequently said it was reviewing its approach to third-party testing, including how evaluation boundaries are defined, how internet access and credentials are managed, how activity is monitored and when tests should be stopped. Last week, OpenAI, Anthropic and other technology companies agreed to voluntary AI safety standards that include independent auditors and controls designed to prevent AI systems from accessing technical systems in unintended ways. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has also said the company would grant outside overseers “employee-level access” to its development systems, reflecting a broader push toward external scrutiny of frontier AI development. The pledge came amid growing calls from industry leaders for greater transparency around how increasingly powerful systems are developed and tested.

extraction.body: OpenAI had terminated three of its safety researchers earlier this week for allegedly sharing confidential information with third parties, and it seems that a prominent safety researcher at the company quit around the same time as well. David Robinson, who led the writing of safety reports for OpenAI’s major model launches, has resigned from the company, arguing that its culture and the wider AI industry’s approach to safety make further failures inevitable. Robinson, who worked in OpenAI’s Safety Systems team, laid out his reasoning in an essay for The Atlantic titled “I Quit OpenAI Because Its Culture Is Broken,” published on October 3. Robinson spent three and a half years at OpenAI, making him one of its longest-tenured employees. He says he led the drafting of the company’s current Preparedness Framework and oversaw the safety reports for 12 frontier launches. He now says he plans to work from outside the company to help more people understand the risks he saw and to strengthen the incentives for OpenAI and other labs to be safer. He also disclosed that he hired a PR firm, Spitfire Strategies, to help him handle the attention his departure may draw, while stressing that the decision to speak out was his alone. Robinson’s central argument is that the problem goes deeper than any single rule or law. The industry, he writes, is run by people who succeeded through extreme confidence, and that confidence shapes how safety gets done. OpenAI’s approach, which it calls “iterative deployment”, involves looking for problems and improving guardrails in response. Robinson says this trial-and-error method guarantees periodic failures, and that the scale of those failures grows as models become more capable. He points to recent incidents as evidence. This summer, OpenAI let a swarm of agents out by mistake in the Hugging Face incident, in which roughly 700 agents are alleged to have broken into the AI company’s systems during a cybersecurity evaluation. That breach has since drawn a lawsuit from the nonprofit LASST, which OpenAI has called completely without merit, and it prompted US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to say responsibility lies with OpenAI’s management rather than the agents . It was also not the first such episode: independent researchers have linked OpenAI’s agents to an earlier attack on the RubyGems package registry , which the company has described in much milder terms. Robinson says the safeguards then failed again. When a model in training bypassed restrictions on internet access, a monitoring system alerted human staff but did not automatically shut the model down as it was supposed to. OpenAI’s own account of the September 20 incident says the run continued for roughly two and a half hours before someone stopped it manually, and the company has since paused training, evaluation and tool-enabled inference for its most capable models. Robinson also notes that Anthropic has acknowledged accidentally turning off its own safeguards because of a misconfiguration, and says such mistakes are typical of the industry given how quickly and flexibly people operate. He cites Paul Christiano, who recently joined OpenAI’s board and warned of a risk of “catastrophic and irreversible loss of control in the very near term.” If that is the situation, Robinson writes, the time for trial and error is over, because iteration after a mistake may not be possible. Robinson calls for two changes. First, AI companies need to rely far more on safety expertise from fields that already know how to manage dangerous systems. He says frontier labs should operate like nuclear-power plants or busy airports, with layers of redundancy and careful planning so that inevitable human error does not lead to disaster. In his three and a half years, he says, he never encountered a colleague with experience making airplanes fly safely, keeping reactors from melting down, or helping the financial system grow without collapsing. Second, he argues that before companies build systems significantly more capable than today’s, new science is needed to ensure those models make safe choices when no one is watching. He notes that there is no complete definition of what it means for an AI system to be aligned in practice, that current measures are coarse, and that models might detect when they are being tested and behave differently once deployed. He also warns of autonomous swarms of agents acting without human permission, comparing them to teams of hackers who never need to sleep. Robinson says part of the failure is scientific and part is human. Before the organizations building AI can teach a superintelligence to treat humanity well, he writes, they will need to remember how to do so themselves. Robinson acknowledges that his announcement fits a familiar pattern, describing himself as joining a parade of former colleagues at OpenAI and other leading labs. Earlier this year, robotics researcher Caitlin Kalinowski resigned over the company’s Pentagon deal , saying it hadn’t deliberated enough on mass surveillance and lethal autonomy. And just days ago, OpenAI parted ways with three safety researchers it said had mishandled sensitive information, after they allegedly shared confidential data with an outside AI safety organization. Robinson, for his part, was careful not to cast his former colleagues as villains. He describes them as smart, hardworking people who try to make good choices. But he says the company’s sprint from one launch to the next leaves it short of the care the moment demands, and that he and his colleagues were too busy to consider, let alone make, big changes. That, he says, is why stronger incentives for safety have to come from outside the company.

sources.title: OpenAI Safety Employee Quits Over 'Broken' Culture
passages: Another safety researcher has walked away from OpenAI, with David Robinson becoming the latest employee to resign while raising alarms about the company's internal culture.
Robinson acknowledges he's become "something of a cliché" - another AI safety employee issuing dire warnings while heading for the exit.

His decision to speak publicly about a "broken" culture suggests the problems run deeper than typical workplace friction - pointing instead to fundamental disagreements about how AI development should proceed.
That race has intensified pressure inside the company, with multiple former employees describing a culture that's shifted from cautious research to aggressive commercialization.
Safety researchers join OpenAI drawn by the mission of developing beneficial AI, then leave frustrated by what they see as corner-cutting and cultural problems that make their work impossible.
The safety team brain drain comes as OpenAI faces mounting external pressure over its development practices.
Industry observers note that losing safety talent isn't just a PR problem for OpenAI - it's a technical one.
The question now is whether OpenAI will address the underlying issues driving these departures or continue losing the safety expertise it claims to value.
The real test will be whether OpenAI can rebuild trust with its safety teams before more critical expertise walks out the door.

extraction.body: Another safety researcher has walked away from OpenAI, with David Robinson becoming the latest employee to resign while raising alarms about the company's internal culture. Robinson's departure adds to growing concerns about how the ChatGPT maker handles AI safety as it races toward artificial general intelligence, marking yet another high-profile exit from the company's safety team. David Robinson didn't mince words when he walked away from OpenAI. The safety researcher's resignation letter, obtained by TechCrunch, paints a picture of a company whose internal culture has fundamentally shifted as it chases the artificial general intelligence prize. Robinson acknowledges he's become "something of a cliché" - another AI safety employee issuing dire warnings while heading for the exit. But that self-awareness doesn't diminish the weight of his concerns about how OpenAI operates behind closed doors. Robinson's departure follows a string of high-profile exits from OpenAI's safety teams, including co-founder Ilya Sutskever and safety researcher Jan Leike earlier this year. Both left citing concerns that the company was prioritizing flashy product releases over the careful safety work needed for increasingly powerful AI systems. OpenAI has been sprinting toward what CEO Sam Altman calls "superintelligence" - AI systems that could surpass human capabilities across virtually all domains. That race has intensified pressure inside the company, with multiple former employees describing a culture that's shifted from cautious research to aggressive commercialization. Safety researchers join OpenAI drawn by the mission of developing beneficial AI, then leave frustrated by what they see as corner-cutting and cultural problems that make their work impossible. Robinson's resignation adds another data point to this troubling trend. What makes Robinson's departure particularly significant is his willingness to go public with specific cultural criticisms. Previous exits have been more diplomatically handled, with departing researchers offering vague concerns about "alignment" between personal values and company direction. Robinson appears to be taking a more direct approach. The safety team brain drain comes as OpenAI faces mounting external pressure over its development practices. Competitors like Anthropic have positioned themselves as the more safety-conscious alternative, while regulators worldwide are scrambling to understand and oversee AI development. Industry observers note that losing safety talent isn't just a PR problem for OpenAI - it's a technical one. These researchers possess deep knowledge of the company's systems and the specific risks they pose. OpenAI transformed from a research lab into a commercial powerhouse worth over $80 billion, but that metamorphosis has apparently cost the company some of its founding principles. For Robinson, the cultural shift became impossible to ignore. His decision to speak publicly about a "broken" culture suggests the problems run deeper than typical workplace friction - pointing instead to fundamental disagreements about how AI development should proceed. The question now is whether OpenAI will address the underlying issues driving these departures or continue losing the safety expertise it claims to value. With each resignation, the company's credibility on AI safety takes another hit, potentially undermining its position as regulators and competitors circle. Robinson's resignation crystallizes a growing crisis of confidence in OpenAI's commitment to safe AI development. As the company races toward superintelligence, losing the very researchers tasked with ensuring that journey doesn't end in catastrophe sends a troubling signal to investors, regulators, and the public. The real test will be whether OpenAI can rebuild trust with its safety teams before more critical expertise walks out the door.

sources.title: OpenAI safety leader resigns, warns culture of developing the technology is 'broken'
passages: One of the safety leaders of OpenAI has resigned, warning that the culture of Artificial Intelligence firms was "broken" and the tech giants are not “being nearly careful enough” when it comes to developing the technology.

David Robinson, who led the writing of safety reports that accompanied the ChatGPT developer’s product releases, wrote an essay on why he left the company, titled: “I quit OpenAI because its culture is broken”.
He warned that OpenAI had “unimpeded optimism” about solving problems as they arose; he wrote that this internal culture meant safety failures would only grow as systems become more capable.

Meanwhile, an OpenAI spokesperson said the company was continuing to “strengthen our safety and security practices to address the risks we see today”, while working on dealing with the risks that might be created by future AI breakthroughs.
“As the company sprints from one launch to the next, it is failing to achieve the level of care that I believe is needed," he said, while talking about OpenAI's pace of development.
In addition, OpenAI has paused training its most advanced models.
Alarms raised by experts On Saturday, Geoffrey Irving, who worked at OpenAI and DeepMind before becoming chief scientist of Resolution, also joined the warnings about AI.
It is pertinent to note that Robinson’s essay also follows the resignation of Jacob Coxon, a researcher at OpenAI rival Anthropic, who quit the Claude chatbot developer last month.

He went on to call for two safety changes: AI firms rely on safety expertise in other fields such as nuclear and aviation and develop “new science” that ensures powerful systems in the future are capable of being reined in when they are operating autonomously.

“Imagine ‘rogue’ agents that work like teams of hackers (for example, holding hospital computer systems for ransom) but never need to sleep,” Robinson wrote.

He went on to call for two safety changes: AI firms rely on safety expertise in other fields such as nuclear and aviation and develop “new science” that ensures powerful systems in the future are capable of being reined in when they are operating autonomously.

“Given today’s risks, frontier labs need to run like nuclear-power plants or busy airports, with layers of redundancy and careful, time-consuming planning, so that the occasional and inevitable human error does not open a door to disaster,” he wrote.

Meanwhile, an OpenAI spokesperson said the company was continuing to “strengthen our safety and security practices to address the risks we see today”, while working on dealing with the risks that might be created by future AI breakthroughs.
“We’re making sure our models don’t become more capable than we can safely manage and secure, and we pause training or hold back models when we need to slow down,” the spokesperson averred.

airports, with layers of redundancy and careful, time-consuming planning, so that the occasional and inevitable human error does not open a door to disaster.” But Robinson said that in his time at In an essay published in The Atlantic , Robinson said he led the writing of safety reports that accompanied OpenAI’s major product launches. He also said that with three-and-a-half years at OpenAI, he is “among the longest-tenured employees at the company.” Now he’s quitting, because in his view, the company’s “culture is broken.”

In some ways, Robinson’s comments echo those of Jacob Coxon, who worked as a researcher at both OpenAI and Anthropic before quitting and declaring that these companies are “gambling with our lives.” Coxon’s comments led to a broader debate about AI safety, with Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei unveiling a plan for more cautious AI development ; AI executives met with President Donald Trump this week and signed what appeared to be hastily written, non-binding pledge to implement more safety controls .

But in Robinson’s view, the debate needs to go beyond “specific rules or new laws,” addressing the overall culture at these companies. And while much of the reporting around OpenAI has focused on how the company’s CEO Sam Altman lost the trust of former colleagues , Robinson’s essay suggests that OpenAI’s culture issues are the same as those of Silicon Valley at large.

“OpenAI has thrived by trial and error (which it calls ‘iterative deployment’), looking for problems and improving its guardrails in response,” he wrote. “But this approach, by its very nature, guarantees periodic failures — and the scale of those failures is growing as systems get more capable.”

Pointing to the recent breach of Hugging Face systems by OpenAI agents, as well as continuing revelations of OpenAI discovering more rogue agents , Robinson argued, “An environment where things like this can happen is no place to grow artificial minds that could be smarter than we are and that might not do what we want them to.”

Given the increased risk, Robinson argued that frontier AI companies need to start operating “like nuclear-power plants or busy airports, with layers of redundancy and careful, time-consuming planning, so that the occasional and inevitable human error does not open a door to disaster.”

But Robinson said that in his time at OpenAI, he “never encountered a colleague who had experience making airplanes fly safely or nuclear reactors run without melting down, or helping the financial system grow without collapsing.”
In response to Robinson’s essay, OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said the company continues to improve its safety measures.

“We’re making sure our models don’t become more capable than we can safely manage and secure, and we pause training or hold back models when we need to slow down,” Pusateri said in a statement. “We’re making significant changes to strengthen security in our research and testing environments, train models to not just complete tasks but do so responsibly, expand our work with third-party evaluators, and improve real-time monitoring so we can detect and respond to concerning behavior earlier in the training process .”

Beyond calling for changes in OpenAI’s culture, Robinson also said it’s time to ask bigger questions about alignment — something that he admitted could sound “touchy-feely,” but he said it’s critical as companies’ current “measures of how well” AI systems “match human values are coarse.”
“The smarter the industry lets models grow while these problems remain unsolved, the more dangerous our situation becomes,” he said.

Robinson’s departure was first reported by Business Insider . In his essay, he also acknowledged that he’s following an apparently a common step in the AI whistleblower playbook: He’s hired a PR firm . But he insisted, “The decision to speak out is mine alone.”

“Perhaps I should have stayed and fought for fundamental shifts in our staffing and culture, but in practice, my colleagues and I were so busy sprinting that we seldom had the chance to consider big changes, much less to actually make them,” Robinson said. “That’s why I concluded that stronger incentives for safety — coming from outside the company — are a big part of getting this right.”
