extraction.body: Another safety researcher has walked away from OpenAI, with David Robinson becoming the latest employee to resign while raising alarms about the company's internal culture. Robinson's departure adds to growing concerns about how the ChatGPT maker handles AI safety as it races toward artificial general intelligence, marking yet another high-profile exit from the company's safety team. David Robinson didn't mince words when he walked away from OpenAI. The safety researcher's resignation letter, obtained by TechCrunch, paints a picture of a company whose internal culture has fundamentally shifted as it chases the artificial general intelligence prize. Robinson acknowledges he's become "something of a cliché" - another AI safety employee issuing dire warnings while heading for the exit. But that self-awareness doesn't diminish the weight of his concerns about how OpenAI operates behind closed doors. Robinson's departure follows a string of high-profile exits from OpenAI's safety teams, including co-founder Ilya Sutskever and safety researcher Jan Leike earlier this year. Both left citing concerns that the company was prioritizing flashy product releases over the careful safety work needed for increasingly powerful AI systems. OpenAI has been sprinting toward what CEO Sam Altman calls "superintelligence" - AI systems that could surpass human capabilities across virtually all domains. That race has intensified pressure inside the company, with multiple former employees describing a culture that's shifted from cautious research to aggressive commercialization. Safety researchers join OpenAI drawn by the mission of developing beneficial AI, then leave frustrated by what they see as corner-cutting and cultural problems that make their work impossible. Robinson's resignation adds another data point to this troubling trend. What makes Robinson's departure particularly significant is his willingness to go public with specific cultural criticisms. Previous exits have been more diplomatically handled, with departing researchers offering vague concerns about "alignment" between personal values and company direction. Robinson appears to be taking a more direct approach. The safety team brain drain comes as OpenAI faces mounting external pressure over its development practices. Competitors like Anthropic have positioned themselves as the more safety-conscious alternative, while regulators worldwide are scrambling to understand and oversee AI development. Industry observers note that losing safety talent isn't just a PR problem for OpenAI - it's a technical one. These researchers possess deep knowledge of the company's systems and the specific risks they pose. OpenAI transformed from a research lab into a commercial powerhouse worth over $80 billion, but that metamorphosis has apparently cost the company some of its founding principles. For Robinson, the cultural shift became impossible to ignore. His decision to speak publicly about a "broken" culture suggests the problems run deeper than typical workplace friction - pointing instead to fundamental disagreements about how AI development should proceed. The question now is whether OpenAI will address the underlying issues driving these departures or continue losing the safety expertise it claims to value. With each resignation, the company's credibility on AI safety takes another hit, potentially undermining its position as regulators and competitors circle. Robinson's resignation crystallizes a growing crisis of confidence in OpenAI's commitment to safe AI development. As the company races toward superintelligence, losing the very researchers tasked with ensuring that journey doesn't end in catastrophe sends a troubling signal to investors, regulators, and the public. The real test will be whether OpenAI can rebuild trust with its safety teams before more critical expertise walks out the door.

sources.title: OpenAI safety leader resigns, warns culture of developing the technology is 'broken'
passages: One of the safety leaders of OpenAI has resigned, warning that the culture of Artificial Intelligence firms was "broken" and the tech giants are not “being nearly careful enough” when it comes to developing the technology.

David Robinson, who led the writing of safety reports that accompanied the ChatGPT developer’s product releases, wrote an essay on why he left the company, titled: “I quit OpenAI because its culture is broken”.
He warned that OpenAI had “unimpeded optimism” about solving problems as they arose; he wrote that this internal culture meant safety failures would only grow as systems become more capable.

Meanwhile, an OpenAI spokesperson said the company was continuing to “strengthen our safety and security practices to address the risks we see today”, while working on dealing with the risks that might be created by future AI breakthroughs.
“As the company sprints from one launch to the next, it is failing to achieve the level of care that I believe is needed," he said, while talking about OpenAI's pace of development.
In addition, OpenAI has paused training its most advanced models.
Alarms raised by experts On Saturday, Geoffrey Irving, who worked at OpenAI and DeepMind before becoming chief scientist of Resolution, also joined the warnings about AI.
It is pertinent to note that Robinson’s essay also follows the resignation of Jacob Coxon, a researcher at OpenAI rival Anthropic, who quit the Claude chatbot developer last month.

He went on to call for two safety changes: AI firms rely on safety expertise in other fields such as nuclear and aviation and develop “new science” that ensures powerful systems in the future are capable of being reined in when they are operating autonomously.

extraction.body: One of the safety leaders of OpenAI has resigned, warning that the culture of Artificial Intelligence firms was "broken" and the tech giants are not “being nearly careful enough” when it comes to developing the technology. David Robinson, who led the writing of safety reports that accompanied the ChatGPT developer’s product releases, wrote an essay on why he left the company, titled: “I quit OpenAI because its culture is broken”. In his statement, Robinson wrote that a cultural overhaul was needed at cutting-edge AI firms and that incidents such as a “swarm” of OpenAI agents – AI programmes operating autonomously without human oversight – attacking the AI startup Hugging Face were “typical of the industry, given the speed and flexibility with which people operate”. “I agree with other recently departed staff that the companies building this technology aren’t being nearly careful enough. But I believe that we need to look deeper than specific rules or new laws. We need to talk about culture," Robinson wrote in the letter published on Saturday. “As the company sprints from one launch to the next, it is failing to achieve the level of care that I believe is needed," he said, while talking about OpenAI's pace of development. However, in recent weeks, OpenAI has shown signs of caution following the Hugging Face incident and the revelation that it has notified more than 100 organisations about rogue agent activity. This week, the firm announced that it was scrapping the release of the next-generation AI model after several researchers raised safety concerns during internal testing. In addition, OpenAI has paused training its most advanced models. Alarms raised by experts On Saturday, Geoffrey Irving, who worked at OpenAI and DeepMind before becoming chief scientist of Resolution, also joined the warnings about AI. In his piece in Time magazine, Irving wrote: "Recent warnings about the potential destructive power of AI are understating the severity of the situation." “I believe there’s about a 50 per cent chance we all die because of the development of smarter-than-human AI systems, and that our actions over the next two to 10 years will determine the outcome," he said. It is pertinent to note that Robinson’s essay also follows the resignation of Jacob Coxon, a researcher at OpenAI rival Anthropic, who quit the Claude chatbot developer last month. After resigning from the firm, he warned that AI “could kill us all by the end of the decade”. After Coxon's warning, Anthropic issued a separate alert that there was more than a 10 per cent chance that AI would wipe out humanity within the next decade. However, critics of such warnings maintained that most of these proclamations are unscientific because they cannot be verified or falsified. In his essay, Robinson wrote that Silicon Valley lacked an awareness of “how to handle dangerous technology” and “what it means to care for people”. He warned that OpenAI had “unimpeded optimism” about solving problems as they arose; he wrote that this internal culture meant safety failures would only grow as systems become more capable. “Imagine ‘rogue’ agents that work like teams of hackers (for example, holding hospital computer systems for ransom) but never need to sleep,” Robinson wrote. He went on to call for two safety changes: AI firms rely on safety expertise in other fields such as nuclear and aviation and develop “new science” that ensures powerful systems in the future are capable of being reined in when they are operating autonomously. “Given today’s risks, frontier labs need to run like nuclear-power plants or busy airports, with layers of redundancy and careful, time-consuming planning, so that the occasional and inevitable human error does not open a door to disaster,” he wrote. Meanwhile, an OpenAI spokesperson said the company was continuing to “strengthen our safety and security practices to address the risks we see today”, while working on dealing with the risks that might be created by future AI breakthroughs. “We’re making sure our models don’t become more capable than we can safely manage and secure, and we pause training or hold back models when we need to slow down,” the spokesperson averred.

Few artificial intelligence (AI) software companies have generated sizzling growth like Palantir Technologies (NASDAQ: PLTR) has. However, the AI stock is priced at a steep premium due to its success. Palantir's shares trade at roughly 82 times forward earnings. Investors seeking the next Palantir-like opportunity may want to shift their focus to another area: quantum computing. This technology is at an earlier stage than AI software, which means the prospects of tremendous gains could be greater. Should you forget Palantir and buy these three quantum computing stocks instead? Missed AI’s "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 15x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we’re only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » Some might be surprised to see Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOG) (NASDAQ: GOOGL) on this list. The company is best known for its Google search engine, YouTube video-sharing service, and Android mobile operating system. But Alphabet has impeccable quantum computing credentials, too. The company's Google Quantum AI unit has racked up multiple impressive wins. For example, its Willow quantum chip performed a calculation in less than five minutes that would take the fastest supercomputers available today 10 septillion (that's 10 followed by 24 zeros) years to handle. Quantum computing is a perfect fit for Alphabet's Google Cloud unit. Google Cloud ranks among the top three cloud platforms and is a top choice for hosting AI applications. If Alphabet achieves its goal of delivering a large error-corrected quantum computer within the decade, Google Cloud's growth could be explosive. Compared to Palantir, Alphabet looks dirt cheap. It's one of the cheapest "Magnificent Seven" stocks , with a forward earnings multiple of 23. Alphabet doesn't have the risk associated with significant reliance on federal government spending as Palantir does, either. If you're looking for a pure-play quantum computing stock, IonQ (NYSE: IONQ) is without question one of the most exciting candidates. The company's revenue soared 287% year over year in the second quarter of 2026 to $80.1 million, marking the fifth consecutive quarter of record results. IonQ isn't just developing quantum computers. It's also focused on quantum networking, quantum sensing, and quantum cybersecurity. The company's recent acquisition of SkyWater Technology, the largest U.S.-based semiconductor foundry, enabled IonQ to become the only vertically integrated full-stack quantum platform provider. Wall Street favors IonQ above Palantir these days. The consensus 12-month price target for Palantir reflects a potential upside of around 7%. But the average analyst price target for IonQ is more than 70% above the current share price. However, there are risks associated with investing in IonQ. The company remains unprofitable. Its valuation is also at a nosebleed level, with shares trading at 54 times trailing 12-month sales (although that's still lower than Palantir's 76.5 sales multiple). At first glance, D-Wave Quantum (NASDAQ: QBTS) might appear to be a less attractive pure-play quantum computing alternative than IonQ. Its stock has performed worse than IonQ's. D-Wave's Q2 revenue was only $3.1 million, with no growth compared to the prior year period. However, D-Wave Quantum nonetheless offers a unique investment proposition. It's the only dual-platform quantum computing company. D-Wave develops quantum annealing technology that is ideally suited for optimization and probabilistic sampling. The company also markets gate-model quantum computers, which use quantum gates similar to Boolean gates in classical computers. Analysts are arguably more excited about D-Wave than they are about IonQ and Palantir. The average price target projects that the stock will more than double over the next 12 months. Of the 17 analysts surveyed by S&P Global (NYSE: SPGI) in September who cover D-Wave, 15 rated the stock as a "buy" or "strong buy." Palantir beats D-Wave Quantum hands down in terms of recent revenue growth. The AI software company is also profitable, while D-Wave isn't. However, D-Wave believes it's well-positioned to be the first to deploy large-scale error-corrected gate-model quantum computers. If the company achieves this goal, it could plausibly be a much bigger winner than Palantir over the next decade. extraction.body: Palantir Technologies has become one of the biggest names in artificial intelligence (AI), but the current boom is creating opportunities well beyond software. Broadcom ( AVGO +3.35% ) is providing hardware that could rival Nvidia 's graphics processing units ( GPUs) , while Applied Digital ( APLD +5.05% ) is building the physical infrastructure that hyperscalers need to run it all. So for investors who are looking for promising AI bets other than Palantir, these two stocks deserve a closer look. Nvidia might dominate the conversation when it comes to GPUs, but Broadcom is becoming an increasingly important player in AI infrastructure . Instead of competing head-on with Nvidia in general-purpose processors, Broadcom specializes in custom chips and networking technology that help some of the biggest companies build their own AI infrastructure. This puts it in a solid position with hyperscalers that are looking to develop chips specifically designed for their AI workloads. The company is already working with major technology companies such as Alphabet , Meta Platforms , and OpenAI, positioning it at the center of the industry's growing demand for custom chips. That demand is already translating into meaningful growth. The company's latest quarterly results showed AI semiconductor revenue more than tripling year over year, and management expects more acceleration in the current quarter. The company also raised its longer-term AI revenue outlook, underscoring its confidence that hyperscalers' data center investments will continue to climb over the next several years. But more importantly, Broadcom's opportunity extends beyond the chips themselves. Its networking technology is used to connect thousands of AI processors into huge computing clusters, giving the company exposure to multiple parts of the AI building boom. Meanwhile, its established software business includes its VMware AI Factory, which makes it easier for customers to deploy and manage AI infrastructure, launch AI models faster, and improve cost efficiency through automation. But chips are only part of the equation. As AI computing requirements continue to grow, the industry also needs to keep adding physical infrastructure. That's where Applied Digital comes into the picture. Applied Digital offers a different way to participate in the AI boom. Instead of designing chips or developing AI models, the company builds and runs the data centers that power AI workloads. It has been expanding its portfolio of AI campuses, attracting major customers through long-term lease agreements that provide it with strong visibility into its future revenues. It has secured three deals with an investment-grade hyperscaler across different campuses, bringing its total contracted capacity to $36 billion. Moreover, Applied Digital continues to make progress on its existing projects. Its Polaris Forge 1 campus in North Dakota has already kicked off operations, and additional capacity will keep coming online as construction continues. The company also secured further financing to expand its data center portfolio, helping turn its pipeline into operational facilities. Another important development was its move to hive off its cloud services business into a new public company, ChronoScale ( CHRN -0.83% ) . This will allow Applied Digital to focus more on developing and running large-scale AI campuses. That should help strengthen its business, especially as hyperscalers race to secure more computing capacity to train and run advanced AI models. Although Broadcom and Applied Digital are in different parts of the AI supply chain, both stand to benefit from the huge investments being made in the technology. For investors who want a steadier way to play the AI theme than Palantir offers, Broadcom's diversified chip and software business, along with its exposure to surging demand for custom AI chips and networking technology, makes it the safer of these two picks. Applied Digital, on the other hand, is the higher-risk, higher-reward option, as it's betting big on building the data centers needed to power the next generation of AI. Which one is the better choice for your portfolio likely depends on how much risk you're willing to take on. Rick Orford has positions in Alphabet and Meta Platforms. extraction.body: Palantir Technologies has become one of the biggest names in artificial intelligence (AI), but the current boom is creating opportunities well beyond software. Broadcom ( AVGO +3.35% ) is providing hardware that could rival Nvidia 's graphics processing units ( GPUs) , while Applied Digital ( APLD +5.05% ) is building the physical infrastructure that hyperscalers need to run it all. So for investors who are looking for promising AI bets other than Palantir, these two stocks deserve a closer look. Nvidia might dominate the conversation when it comes to GPUs, but Broadcom is becoming an increasingly important player in AI infrastructure . Instead of competing head-on with Nvidia in general-purpose processors, Broadcom specializes in custom chips and networking technology that help some of the biggest companies build their own AI infrastructure. This puts it in a solid position with hyperscalers that are looking to develop chips specifically designed for their AI workloads. The company is already working with major technology companies such as Alphabet , Meta Platforms , and OpenAI, positioning it at the center of the industry's growing demand for custom chips. That demand is already translating into meaningful growth. The company's latest quarterly results showed AI semiconductor revenue more than tripling year over year, and management expects more acceleration in the current quarter. The company also raised its longer-term AI revenue outlook, underscoring its confidence that hyperscalers' data center investments will continue to climb over the next several years. But more importantly, Broadcom's opportunity extends beyond the chips themselves. Its networking technology is used to connect thousands of AI processors into huge computing clusters, giving the company exposure to multiple parts of the AI building boom. Meanwhile, its established software business includes its VMware AI Factory, which makes it easier for customers to deploy and manage AI infrastructure, launch AI models faster, and improve cost efficiency through automation. But chips are only part of the equation. As AI computing requirements continue to grow, the industry also needs to keep adding physical infrastructure. That's where Applied Digital comes into the picture. Applied Digital offers a different way to participate in the AI boom. Instead of designing chips or developing AI models, the company builds and runs the data centers that power AI workloads. It has been expanding its portfolio of AI campuses, attracting major customers through long-term lease agreements that provide it with strong visibility into its future revenues. sources.title: We Asked ChatGPT, Claude and Grok If Citi’s $113,000 Bitcoin Target Arrives Before October 2027 - Yahoo Finance
passages: Citi raised its one-year price target for Bitcoin (CRYPTO:BTC) to $113,000, a significant jump from the $82,000 estimate made in July.
This price increase is exciting, especially since Bitcoin was trading at $84,621 as of October 3, making the target about 34% higher.
ChatGPT gives Bitcoin a 68% chance of hitting Citi's $113,000 target by October 2027, while Claude and Grok put the odds at just 46% and 38%.
All models also projected downside scenarios below Bitcoin's current price.
These figures range from 8% to 20% lower than the current price of $84,621.
All three AI models agreed that $5 billion in fund inflows is insufficient, with two models predicting the chances of success to be below 50%.
Furthermore, Bitcoin is down 30% over the past year, suggesting it will need more buying pressure than Citi anticipates.
Only ChatGPT forecasted a 12-month Bitcoin price above Citi's target, suggesting it could reach $118,000.
Claude projected $104,000, and Grok came in lower at $96,000.
So, the question remains: will Citi's prediction hold up? (FLAG: colon in "the question remains:")
If inflows exceed ChatGPT's upper estimate of $10 billion and Bitcoin trades above $100,000 consistently by March 2027, the target could become achievable.

Conversely, if the Fed opts for another rate hike on October 28 and inflows trend closer to Citi's estimate of $5 billion, Bitcoin could drift into the lower price range suggested by the models, landing between $67,500 and $78,000.
On the other hand, Claude estimated the requirement at about $14 billion, while Grok estimated it at around $15 billion.
For context, before Citi's note, spot Bitcoin ETFs brought in $2.4 billion in just one week—nearly half of Citi's full-year target.
Claude based its analysis on Bitcoin's volatility, estimating annual swings of 45% to 50%.
Each AI model identified a restrictive Federal Reserve as the biggest threat to Bitcoin's growth.
The Fed raised interest rates to a range of 3.75% to 4.00% on September 16, marking its first hike since 2023.
ChatGPT indicated that about $6 billion would be needed, deeming Citi's forecast marginal.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
The crux is that fund flows and the Federal Reserve's actions, rather than Citi's headline number, will dictate the timeline for achieving the target

passages: ChatGPT and Grok both believe Solana (CRYPTO: SOL) will reach $150 before Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC) reaches $100,000, even though the numbers show Solana has farther to go.
We asked both AI models the same question about Solana's price prediction, and they both favored Solana despite its tougher challenge.
On Bitcoin, the models are nearly in agreement.
ChatGPT sees Bitcoin reaching $100,000 in November, finishing the year at $96,000, while Grok predicts it will hit $100,000 in December and end the year at $97,500.
Both models expect Bitcoin to touch $100,000 before ending 2026 below that mark.
For Solana holders, this suggests caution, as Grok's analysis implies that reaching $150 might lead to a temporary peak.
Meanwhile, Bitcoin needs to test its recent high of $87,397 from late September, which is about 3% higher than its current price.
On October 1, 2026, Solana was priced at $118, while Bitcoin was at $84,721.
This meant Solana needed to rise by 27.1%, while Bitcoin needed to climb 18%.
ChatGPT acknowledged that Bitcoin had the easier climb but still gave Solana a 68% chance of hitting $150 first.
Grok took a more cautious stance, estimating a 58% chance.
Solana's volatility runs 1.8 times that of Bitcoin and its funds have pulled in $522 million over 11 straight weeks of inflows.
As of October 3, Solana trades around $119, and Bitcoin is near $84,621, meaning Solana has to gain 25.6%, while Bitcoin faces a climb of 18.2%.
While both models agree on who is likely to reach their target first, they differ on timing and price predictions for Solana.
It predicts a steady climb from $130 to $135, then $145 to $150, followed by a rise to $165.
However, the competition is tighter than ChatGPT's 68% suggests, since one major issuer contributed significantly to Solana's record inflow week.
Both models voiced that if Bitcoin funds draw in over $1 billion weekly while Solana funds see outflows, the predictions could shift dramatically.

For context, before Citi’s note, spot Bitcoin ETFs brought in $2.4 billion in just one week—nearly half of Citi’s full-year target.
Claude based its analysis on Bitcoin’s volatility, estimating annual swings of 45% to 50%.

Citi raised its one-year price target for Bitcoin ( CRYPTO:BTC ) to $113,000, a significant jump from the $82,000 estimate made in July. This price increase is exciting, especially since Bitcoin was trading at $84,621 as of October 3, making the target about 34% higher. Curious about whether Bitcoin can hit Citi’s $113,000 target by October 2027, 24/7 Wall St. consulted three AI models : ChatGPT, Claude, and Grok. (FLAG: “This price increase is exciting” is hype; colon before the model names; “was trading” is past tense for a current price) The responses were quite varied. ChatGPT estimated a 68% chance that Bitcoin would reach Citi’s target, while Claude placed it at 46%, and Grok at 38%. Only ChatGPT forecasted a 12-month Bitcoin price above Citi’s target, suggesting it could reach $118,000. Claude projected $104,000, and Grok came in lower at $96,000. So, the question remains: will Citi’s prediction hold up? (FLAG: colon in “the question remains:”) Along with its target, Citi also projected $5 billion in new inflows into crypto funds within the year. These inflows come from investors adding money to funds like spot Bitcoin ETFs, which purchase and hold Bitcoin for their clients. However, all three AI models concluded that $5 billion alone is not enough to drive Bitcoin to $113,000. (FLAG: gerund opener “Accompanying”) The models provided different estimates of the inflow needed. ChatGPT indicated that about $6 billion would be needed, deeming Citi’s forecast marginal. It suggested that $8 billion to $10 billion could make reaching the target much more feasible. On the other hand, Claude estimated the requirement at about $14 billion, while Grok estimated it at around $15 billion. For context, before Citi’s note, spot Bitcoin ETFs brought in $2.4 billion in just one week—nearly half of Citi’s full-year target. Each AI model identified a restrictive Federal Reserve as the biggest threat to Bitcoin’s growth. The Fed raised interest rates to a range of 3.75% to 4.00% on September 16, marking its first hike since 2023. Claude pointed toward the possibility of another rate hike during the Fed’s meeting on October 27-28, while Grok noted that such increases could reverse the weaker dollar that underpins the bullish outlook for Bitcoin. All models also projected downside scenarios below Bitcoin’s current price. If Citi’s target doesn’t materialize, ChatGPT sees Bitcoin dropping to around $72,000 by October 2027, while Claude estimates $78,000 and Grok anticipates $67,500. These figures range from 8% to 20% lower than the current price of $84,621. The varying estimates stem from the different methods each AI model used. Though they all started with the same question and price point, their approaches led to significant differences. Claude based its analysis on Bitcoin’s volatility, estimating annual swings of 45% to 50%. After using a basic model, it settled on a 46% probability, predicting Bitcoin would first reach $100,000 in March 2027 and then $113,000 by August 2027. ChatGPT focused on momentum and Bitcoin’s proximity to $100,000. It expects Bitcoin to hit $100,000 in November 2026 and reach $113,000 by January 2027, viewing Citi’s $5 billion estimate as the lower end of a reasonable inflow expectation. Grok examined interest rates and overall fund flows compared to Bitcoin’s total market value. It noted that $5 billion in inflows represents only about 0.3% of Bitcoin’s $1.7 trillion market cap. Grok expects Bitcoin to reach $100,000 in December 2026, before ultimately hitting $113,000 in March 2027. Based on Citi’s own inflow forecast, the likelihood of Bitcoin reaching its $113,000 target before October 2027 seems low. All three AI models agreed that $5 billion in fund inflows is insufficient, with two models predicting the chances of success to be below 50%. Furthermore, Bitcoin is down 30% over the past year, suggesting it will need more buying pressure than Citi anticipates. The crux is that fund flows and the Federal Reserve’s actions, rather than Citi’s headline number, will dictate the timeline for achieving the target If inflows exceed ChatGPT’s upper estimate of $10 billion and Bitcoin trades above $100,000 consistently by March 2027, the target could become achievable. Conversely, if the Fed opts for another rate hike on October 28 and inflows trend closer to Citi’s estimate of $5 billion, Bitcoin could drift into the lower price range suggested by the models, landing between $67,500 and $78,000. All three AI models agreed that $5 billion in fund inflows is insufficient, with two models predicting the chances of success to be below 50%.

For context, before Citi’s note, spot Bitcoin ETFs brought in $2.4 billion in just one week—nearly half of Citi’s full-year target.
Claude based its analysis on Bitcoin’s volatility, estimating annual swings of 45% to 50%.

Citi raised its one-year price target for Bitcoin ( CRYPTO:BTC ) to $113,000, a significant jump from the $82,000 estimate made in July. This price increase is exciting, especially since Bitcoin was trading at $84,621 as of October 3, making the target about 34% higher. Curious about whether Bitcoin can hit Citi’s $113,000 target by October 2027, 24/7 Wall St. consulted three AI models : ChatGPT, Claude, and Grok. (FLAG: “This price increase is exciting” is hype; colon before the model names; “was trading” is past tense for a current price) The responses were quite varied. ChatGPT estimated a 68% chance that Bitcoin would reach Citi’s target, while Claude placed it at 46%, and Grok at 38%. Only ChatGPT forecasted a 12-month Bitcoin price above Citi’s target, suggesting it could reach $118,000. Claude projected $104,000, and Grok came in lower at $96,000. So, the question remains: will Citi’s prediction hold up? (FLAG: colon in “the question remains:”) Along with its target, Citi also projected $5 billion in new inflows into crypto funds within the year. These inflows come from investors adding money to funds like spot Bitcoin ETFs, which purchase and hold Bitcoin for their clients. However, all three AI models concluded that $5 billion alone is not enough to drive Bitcoin to $113,000. (FLAG: gerund opener “Accompanying”) The models provided different estimates of the inflow needed. ChatGPT indicated that about $6 billion would be needed, deeming Citi’s forecast marginal. It suggested that $8 billion to $10 billion could make reaching the target much more feasible. On the other hand, Claude estimated the requirement at about $14 billion, while Grok estimated it at around $15 billion. For context, before Citi’s note, spot Bitcoin ETFs brought in $2.4 billion in just one week—nearly half of Citi’s full-year target. Each AI model identified a restrictive Federal Reserve as the biggest threat to Bitcoin’s growth. The Fed raised interest rates to a range of 3.75% to 4.00% on September 16, marking its first hike since 2023. Claude pointed toward the possibility of another rate hike during the Fed’s meeting on October 27-28, while Grok noted that such increases could reverse the weaker dollar that underpins the bullish outlook for Bitcoin. All models also projected downside scenarios below Bitcoin’s current price. If Citi’s target doesn’t materialize, ChatGPT sees Bitcoin dropping to around $72,000 by October 2027, while Claude estimates $78,000 and Grok anticipates $67,500. These figures range from 8% to 20% lower than the current price of $84,621. The varying estimates stem from the different methods each AI model used. Though they all started with the same question and price point, their approaches led to significant differences. Claude based its analysis on Bitcoin’s volatility, estimating annual swings of 45% to 50%. After using a basic model, it settled on a 46% probability, predicting Bitcoin would first reach $100,000 in March 2027 and then $113,000 by August 2027. ChatGPT focused on momentum and Bitcoin’s proximity to $100,000. It expects Bitcoin to hit $100,000 in November 2026 and reach $113,000 by January 2027, viewing Citi’s $5 billion estimate as the lower end of a reasonable inflow expectation. Grok examined interest rates and overall fund flows compared to Bitcoin’s total market value. It noted that $5 billion in inflows represents only about 0.3% of Bitcoin’s $1.7 trillion market cap. Grok expects Bitcoin to reach $100,000 in December 2026, before ultimately hitting $113,000 in March 2027. Based on Citi’s own inflow forecast, the likelihood of Bitcoin reaching its $113,000 target before October 2027 seems low. All three AI models agreed that $5 billion in fund inflows is insufficient, with two models predicting the chances of success to be below 50%. Furthermore, Bitcoin is down 30% over the past year, suggesting it will need more buying pressure than Citi anticipates. The crux is that fund flows and the Federal Reserve’s actions, rather than Citi’s headline number, will dictate the timeline for achieving the target If inflows exceed ChatGPT’s upper estimate of $10 billion and Bitcoin trades above $100,000 consistently by March 2027, the target could become achievable. Conversely, if the Fed opts for another rate hike on October 28 and inflows trend closer to Citi’s estimate of $5 billion, Bitcoin could drift into the lower price range suggested by the models, landing between $67,500 and $78,000. This price increase is exciting, especially since Bitcoin was trading at $84,621 as of October 3, making the target about 34% higher.
All models also projected downside scenarios below Bitcoin’s current price.
If Citi’s target doesn’t materialize, ChatGPT sees Bitcoin dropping to around $72,000 by October 2027, while Claude estimates $78,000 and Grok anticipates $67,500.
These figures range from 8% to 20% lower than the current price of $84,621.
All three AI models agreed that $5 billion in fund inflows is insufficient, with two models predicting the chances of success to be below 50%.
Furthermore, Bitcoin is down 30% over the past year, suggesting it will need more buying pressure than Citi anticipates.
So, the question remains: will Citi’s prediction hold up? (FLAG: colon in “the question remains:”)
If inflows exceed ChatGPT’s upper estimate of $10 billion and Bitcoin trades above $100,000 consistently by March 2027, the target could become achievable.
On the other hand, Claude estimated the requirement at about $14 billion, while Grok estimated it at around $15 billion.
For context, before Citi’s note, spot Bitcoin ETFs brought in $2.4 billion in just one week—nearly half of Citi’s full-year target.
Claude based its analysis on Bitcoin’s volatility, estimating annual swings of 45% to 50%.
Sam Daodu is a crypto analyst who's spent nearly a decade making blockchain understandable—no easy task when most whitepapers read like fever dreams.
He writes for 24/7 Wall St., covering Bitcoin, altcoins, and crypto market analysis for investors.
Before crypto, he was a tech writer (back when explaining "the cloud" was peak innovation).
Since 2018, he's written for CoinTelegraph, Yahoo Finance, The Block, Cryptonews, Zypto, Rain, and more—basically anywhere people want crypto news without the headache.
Sam runs MacLabs Marketing, a content agency for crypto brands tired of sounding like AI wrote their website.
He also publishes free crypto education on his site for Web3 enthusiasts who think "gas fees" is a typo.

When he's not writing or staring at charts, Sam's either: - Watching anime (currently convinced One Piece has better tokenomics than most altcoins) - At the gym sculpting himself into a Greek god - Listening to the music your mum warned you only bad boys listen to Connect: LinkedIn | Email | MacLabs Marketing
Each AI model identified a restrictive Federal Reserve as the biggest threat to Bitcoin’s growth.
The Fed raised interest rates to a range of 3.75% to 4.00% on September 16, marking its first hike since 2023.

Claude pointed toward the possibility of another rate hike during the Fed’s meeting on October 27-28, while Grok noted that such increases could reverse the weaker dollar that underpins the bullish outlook for Bitcoin.
ChatGPT, Claude, and Grok all called Bitcoin a buy at current prices, but not one of them would say the bottom is in, and their worst-case targets reveal a sharp split over how far…
We asked ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, and DeepSeek the same question: What will XRP (CRYPTO: XRP) be worth by the end of 2026?
Their answers ranged from $1.4 to $14, marking a 10x gap between…
ChatGPT indicated that about $6 billion would be needed, deeming Citi’s forecast marginal.
ChatGPT and Grok both backed Solana over Bitcoin in a race to their respective price targets, even though Solana faces a steeper climb.
The crux is that fund flows and the Federal Reserve’s actions, rather than Citi’s headline number, will dictate the timeline for achieving the target
Citigroup just issued a bold new Bitcoin price target based on surprisingly modest assumptions, but its own track record in 2026 reveals how quickly that forecast could collapse.

extraction.body: The White House is blocking CNN from flying aboard Air Force One on Saturday, preventing the network from carrying out its duties covering President Donald Trump on behalf of the other major networks. According to multiple media reports , including CNN's own , the network was slated to travel with the president to Tennessee for a college football game as part of the White House TV press pool. The decision to bar CNN from the flight was reportedly shared Friday evening in a note that laid out Trump's schedule. It's said no outlet had been listed as a replacement for CNN, implying that there will be no TV pool coverage for his trip to Tennessee. A representative for the White House did not immediately respond to TheWrap's request for comment. The update comes a day after CNN, MS NOW and Politico regained their White House credentials under a court order , following Trump's ban on the outlets last week. The drama all started last Friday, when Trump took to Truth Social and shared that he was banning the three outlets from the White House for "constantly" writing negatively about his administration. "Media Outlets shouldn't be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they're covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America," Trump wrote at the time. "Other Fake News Media Outlets to follow." He doubled down on his sentiment while speaking to reporters that same day, noting, "I don't think a court should allow fake news to be written day after day after day. I think that somebody has a right to keep them away if they're going to write false stories all the time." Trump added: "There's something wrong with a country that can allow people to purposely tell negative stories … if they want to write them, that's fine, but I don't have to let them into my, into the people's house." Then, on Monday, CNN, Politico and MS NOW sued President Trump and his administration after their reporters were stripped of their White House access and credentials. "This morning, we notified the government that we are filing a lawsuit today to protect our First Amendment rights and defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes," the outlets shared in a joint statement on Monday. "Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists' credentials because it objected to our reporting. Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public's right to independent journalism free from government interference." Not only did the outlets file a complaint and a memorandum of law in D.C. District Court, they also filed a motion for a temporary restraining order. However, the president stood firm in his decision on Monday, once again bemoaning in a follow-up Truth Social post that the outlets only write "negatively" about him. "It is called the Oval Office, and it should be treated with Decorum, Respect, and Dignity, not defiled by Third Rate Clowns, who purposefully distort, twist, and degrade with everything they write or publish," he wrote. "Virtually every story about me, or anything having to do with me, is negative, wrong and, in many cases, DANGEROUS for our Country! No matter how GREAT my Achievements, they trivialize and demean. The fact is, I won all seven Swing States, the Popular Vote, the Electoral College (312 to 226), and the Counties throughout America by 86%, and yet it is reported that I get 94% bad publicity. With such a Crooked and Corrupt Press, how did I win in such a LANDSLIDE? It is because the Media has NO credibility, and that is a very bad thing for our Nation! Why should I have to give 'access' to such people? Perhaps Judge Kelly could explain that! In any event, I have an obligation to fight for the Success and Safety of our Country. FAKE NEWS IS A THREAT TO DEMOCRACY, and I will do whatever is necessary to make sure that the U.S.A. thrives." In the early morning hours Thursday, U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly ordered the White House to reinstate credentials for reporters at CNN, MS NOW and Politico. However, it wasn't until noon that day that reporters were able to regain access. In fact, CNN correspondent Betsy Klein and MS NOW White House correspondent Laura Barrón-López both shared Thursday that they were turned away several times before being let back into the White House. Additionally, Judge Kelly declined the administration's request to delay the order from taking effect. The TRO is set to run for 14 days while the court moves to expedited briefing on the outlets' request for a preliminary injunction. Apparently, this is a series that would undoubtedly get NewsOne banned from the White House press corps, not because we’re lying about the lying-est president in recent history, but because Trump’s orangey-white supremacist butt gets hurt when the overwhelming majority of news outlets fail to report anything positive about him, which is pretty much always, and for the same reason virtually no media outlets would report anything positive about fire, brimstone, and flying locusts filling the skies. Anyway, let’s get into it… Trump Defends White House Ban On CNN, MS NOW and Politico, As Outlets Sue Over 1st Amendment Attack The most annoying thing about Trump’s constant attacks on the free press, including his recent banning of CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House, is that he is so obviously and demonstrably the “fake news” he has spent the last decade complaining about. Look, all politicians lie, but Trump is in a league of his own when it comes to his reliance on propaganda as virtually his only mode of communication. Trump doesn’t just lie; he lies compulsively, and they’re consistently the most absurd, easily fact-checked lies told by any politician in any of our lifetimes, which, of course, is saying a lot. 6 — Trump’s entire existence as a U.S. president has been a 24/7, 365 detachment from any semblance of what’s going on in the real world. Since he announced the ban, Trump hasn’t once mentioned a specific grievance with any of the three outlets. He hasn’t mentioned a single lie they told about him; he’s only vaguely declared that “Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States.” And that hasn’t changed now that he’s claiming he is not attacking the free press; he also banned the free press. “The White House is not instituting an assault on the Free Press, something which I cherish,” he posted on Truth Social on Monday. “It is instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS, something that has grown like Cancer in our beloved United States of America. It is a threat to our National Security, and must be stopped, NOW!” Of course, that was after he told reporters in the White House that “the ban on the free press” was happening, which may or may not have been a Freudian slip. On Monday, CNN, MS NOW and Politico filed a joint First Amendment lawsuit to restore their access to the White House, arguing that “this ban could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment nor a more blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles,” which could result in the federal courts stepping in, just as one did when the Pentagon tried to implement its own free speech-defying press policy, which virtually every mainstream media outlet — including conservative outlets like Newsmax and Fox News — responded to with a resounding “hell no,” leading to the policy being ruled unconstitutional. Speaking of Newsmax and Fox News, notice there’s no concern that those outlets, which have been successfully sued for peddling MAGA propaganda, might be banned from the White House. Trump is even out here touting Breitbart News — yes, that Breitbart News — as its beacon of truth and “the only outlet that covers him fairly.” Come on, y’all — this is a man who loves “fake news,” is “fake news,” and relies on “fake news” as his only political refuge. He’s just mad because media outlets won’t lie for him. Meanwhile, according to USA Today, major TV networks have decided to suspend their own White House pool coverage in protest of Trump’s ban, including ABC, CBS, NBC, and Fox News — yes, that Fox News. Trump, the president who never met an expert he didn’t want to undermine in the name of MAGA science, responded by calling it all a big, all-caps-worthy “HOAX,” while fancying himself a “Hoax Buster.” Again, Mr. It would be the perfect example of Trump Intelligence, which is, if nothing else, artificial. Speaking of AI, Trump’s love affair with AI slop continues to be an every-hour-on-the-hour thing, as do his self-revealed fantasies of global authoritarianism. In the image, the only nation clearly shown is Greenland, which likely means this post was inspired by the new Greenland deal he’s been boasting about, even though it’s the same deal we have had with the nation for 75 years, with a few more bells and whistles. “I am pleased to announce that the United States of America has entered into an Agreement with The Kingdom of Denmark, and Greenland, that gives the United States permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland, completely addressing ALL of our many U.S. concerns,” Trump claimed in a lengthy social media post. The U.S. has had a deal allowing it a largely unfettered military presence in Greenland since 1951, but the new deal is reportedly different because it makes U.S. military presence in the region permanent, according to Trump, and bars non-NATO nations from establishing their own presence in Greenland. Trump Still Thinks He’s Currently Serving A Third Term Earlier this year, Trump declared that “anybody running for President or Vice President should be forced to take a Cognitive Examination,” which seemed to be based on the fact that his own doctors keep making him take cognitive exams, which he doesn’t seem to know isn’t a thing that speaks to him being of sound mind. He also didn’t seem to understand that calling his current term “THREE” undermined the message he was going for. On Friday, Trump posted what he called his “TOP 25 TRUMP ACCOMPLISHMENTS OF TERM THREE,” which included the termination of “scams” that only he has declared a scam, like the green energy efforts he has long declared war on, the “8 wars” he keeps claiming he ended without giving explicit examples, his National Guard deployments, which have largely been blocked by federal judges, including SCOTUS, because they’re unconstitutional, and the aforementioned drop in crime that he is in no way responsible for. Of course, Trump lying about his non-accomplishments is just par for the MAGA course, but his insistence that he’s actually served three terms because he still can’t handle his loss in 2020 should be a concern to anyone who wants to believe the nation isn’t being run by a poster child for mental health awareness for senior citizens. passages: Less than a week since Donald Trump proudly announced that CNN, MS NOW, and Politico would be banned from the White House, a federal judge reinstated the news organizations’ press credentials by granting a temporary restraining order.

extraction.body: The White House is blocking CNN from flying aboard Air Force One on Saturday, preventing the network from carrying out its duties covering President Donald Trump on behalf of the other major networks. According to multiple media reports , including CNN's own , the network was slated to travel with the president to Tennessee for a college football game as part of the White House TV press pool. The decision to bar CNN from the flight was reportedly shared Friday evening in a note that laid out Trump's schedule. It's said no outlet had been listed as a replacement for CNN, implying that there will be no TV pool coverage for his trip to Tennessee. A representative for the White House did not immediately respond to TheWrap's request for comment. The update comes a day after CNN, MS NOW and Politico regained their White House credentials under a court order , following Trump's ban on the outlets last week. The drama all started last Friday, when Trump took to Truth Social and shared that he was banning the three outlets from the White House for "constantly" writing negatively about his administration. "Media Outlets shouldn't be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they're covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America," Trump wrote at the time. "Other Fake News Media Outlets to follow." He doubled down on his sentiment while speaking to reporters that same day, noting, "I don't think a court should allow fake news to be written day after day after day. I think that somebody has a right to keep them away if they're going to write false stories all the time." Trump added: "There's something wrong with a country that can allow people to purposely tell negative stories … if they want to write them, that's fine, but I don't have to let them into my, into the people's house." Then, on Monday, CNN, Politico and MS NOW sued President Trump and his administration after their reporters were stripped of their White House access and credentials. "This morning, we notified the government that we are filing a lawsuit today to protect our First Amendment rights and defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes," the outlets shared in a joint statement on Monday. "Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists' credentials because it objected to our reporting. Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public's right to independent journalism free from government interference." Not only did the outlets file a complaint and a memorandum of law in D.C. District Court, they also filed a motion for a temporary restraining order. However, the president stood firm in his decision on Monday, once again bemoaning in a follow-up Truth Social post that the outlets only write "negatively" about him. "It is called the Oval Office, and it should be treated with Decorum, Respect, and Dignity, not defiled by Third Rate Clowns, who purposefully distort, twist, and degrade with everything they write or publish," he wrote. "Virtually every story about me, or anything having to do with me, is negative, wrong and, in many cases, DANGEROUS for our Country! No matter how GREAT my Achievements, they trivialize and demean. The fact is, I won all seven Swing States, the Popular Vote, the Electoral College (312 to 226), and the Counties throughout America by 86%, and yet it is reported that I get 94% bad publicity. With such a Crooked and Corrupt Press, how did I win in such a LANDSLIDE? It is because the Media has NO credibility, and that is a very bad thing for our Nation! Why should I have to give 'access' to such people? Perhaps Judge Kelly could explain that! In any event, I have an obligation to fight for the Success and Safety of our Country. Trump Still Thinks He’s Currently Serving A Third Term Earlier this year, Trump declared that “anybody running for President or Vice President should be forced to take a Cognitive Examination,” which seemed to be based on the fact that his own doctors keep making him take cognitive exams, which he doesn’t seem to know isn’t a thing that speaks to him being of sound mind. sources.title: CNN, MS NOW, and Politico Regain White House Access After Court Order - New York Magazine
passages: Less than a week since Donald Trump proudly announced that CNN, MS NOW, and Politico would be banned from the White House, a federal judge reinstated the news organizations’ press credentials by granting a temporary restraining order.
By midmorning Thursday, several hours after the court order came down, reporters from the three organizations all said they were still being barred from entry, causing a furor in the press corps.
Both the New York Times and the Associated Press have previously won legal victories over press restrictions at the Pentagon and White House, respectively, though both cases remain in litigation.
It was expected that Judge Kelly — who reinstated former CNN correspondent Jim Acosta’s White House credentials in 2018 — would similarly do so in this case.

As Elie Honig explained on Wednesday morning, ahead of an afternoon hearing, “The First Amendment doesn’t care if Trump gets bad press.” Even Trump appeared resigned to lose, writing on Truth Social this week that “almost without question and, as usual, we’ll go for appeal.”
The result was a Veep -like debacle on Monday as Trump could barely be heard during his ribbon-cutting ceremony for a new White House helipad.
News organizations demonstrated solidarity in other ways, such as temporarily withholding still photography , and dozens signed an amicus brief in support of the three banished outlets.

Less than a week since Donald Trump proudly announced that CNN, MS NOW, and Politico would be banned from the White House, a federal judge reinstated the news organizations’ press credentials by granting a temporary restraining order. By midmorning Thursday, several hours after the court order came down, reporters from the three organizations all said they were still being barred from entry, causing a furor in the press corps. Eventually, the White House complied with the order and permitted entry. U.S. district judge Timothy Kelly ruled that the outlets would likely succeed on Fifth Amendment grounds given that their passes were “revoked without constitutionally adequate due process.” The judge, who was appointed by Trump during his first term, wasn’t swayed by the Justice Department’s arguments about national-security concerns that it leveled days after Trump indicated he was yanking the passes because he didn’t like the outlets’ “fake news” reporting. “The Court is skeptical — at least on this record — that Defendants’ interest in safeguarding national security is the actual motivation for, or is even advanced by, the revocation of Plaintiffs’ hard passes,” wrote Kelly, who noted that some of the reporting identified stretched “back months or years” and some stories appeared routine. “Nothing in the record that predates this suit suggests that the revocation of Plaintiffs’ hard passes was motivated by national security concerns,” he added. “Certainly, that is not what President Trump said when he announced that he was ‘banning’ Plaintiffs from the White House — instead, he focused on the alleged lack of truthfulness and negativity of Plaintiffs’ reporting.” Attorney Ted Boutrous, who represented the media outlets, applauded the decision, “This is a strong ruling vindicating freedom of the press, due process, and the rule of law. We greatly appreciate the court’s swift action.” It was expected that Judge Kelly — who reinstated former CNN correspondent Jim Acosta’s White House credentials in 2018 — would similarly do so in this case. As Elie Honig explained on Wednesday morning, ahead of an afternoon hearing, “The First Amendment doesn’t care if Trump gets bad press.” Even Trump appeared resigned to lose, writing on Truth Social this week that “almost without question and, as usual, we’ll go for appeal.” The press ban quickly backfired on Trump, as major networks declined to participate in the rotating television pool that covers the president given that one member, CNN, had been banned. The result was a Veep -like debacle on Monday as Trump could barely be heard during his ribbon-cutting ceremony for a new White House helipad. News organizations demonstrated solidarity in other ways, such as temporarily withholding still photography , and dozens signed an amicus brief in support of the three banished outlets. “This is a historic moment,” MS NOW White House reporter Akayla Gardner said Thursday on the network. “We have President Xi coming here to Washington for a major state visit, and at this moment, we’re seeing tremendous solidarity amongst the news outlets.” Judge Kelly’s temporary restraining order stays in effect for 14 days, as the court will next move to consider a preliminary injunction. The judge may fully address the media outlets’ First Amendment arguments at that later day. Both the New York Times and the Associated Press have previously won legal victories over press restrictions at the Pentagon and White House, respectively, though both cases remain in litigation. relevantPassages.text: Less than a week since Donald Trump proudly announced that CNN, MS NOW, and Politico would be banned from the White House, a federal judge reinstated the news organizations’ press credentials by granting a temporary restraining order.
By midmorning Thursday, several hours after the court order came down, reporters from the three organizations all said they were still being barred from entry, causing a furor in the press corps.
Both the New York Times and the Associated Press have previously won legal victories over press restrictions at the Pentagon and White House, respectively, though both cases remain in litigation.
It was expected that Judge Kelly — who reinstated former CNN correspondent Jim Acosta’s White House credentials in 2018 — would similarly do so in this case.

As Elie Honig explained on Wednesday morning, ahead of an afternoon hearing, “The First Amendment doesn’t care if Trump gets bad press.” Even Trump appeared resigned to lose, writing on Truth Social this week that “almost without question and, as usual, we’ll go for appeal.”
The result was a Veep -like debacle on Monday as Trump could barely be heard during his ribbon-cutting ceremony for a new White House helipad.
News organizations demonstrated solidarity in other ways, such as temporarily withholding still photography , and dozens signed an amicus brief in support of the three banished outlets.

"The president asked that a group be put together," which the administration refers to as the "Super Intelligence Force," to ensure the US remains a leader in advanced AI while protecting Americans' interests, Clayton told the ‌Journal, adding that "the risk of ⁠not being first is high." The safety of AI has become a major issue in recent weeks, with some researchers warning that people ⁠building the technology believe it could kill humans within a decade. Several Democratic and Republican lawmakers have responded with alarm and calls for more action. Clayton's panel will review AI-related risks and current government reporting mechanisms for breaches, hacks and other incidents, and recommend ways to strengthen federal-response capabilities under existing authorities, the Journal said, citing the task force's charter. This is the ‌second time Trump has named an adviser to ​oversee AI-related decisions across the administration. Venture capitalist ​David Sacks held the AI czar ​role at the beginning of Trump's second term. The task force's vice ‌chairs will be Emil Michael, Scott ​Kupor and Federal Trade ​Commission Chair Andrew Ferguson, while members will include Vice President JD Vance, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and White House Chief of Staff ​Susie Wiles, according to ‌the report. passages: The task force has been named the ‘Super Intelligence Force’, Trump’s preferred name for AI

A NEW White House task force will produce a report assessing risks posed by artificial intelligence and what responsibility the US federal government should have over the technology, the Wall Street Journal reported.

The task force will be led by US director of national intelligence Jay Clayton, who confirmed his role to the paper. The role makes Clayton effectively the Trump administration’s new AI czar, a senior White House official told the Wall Street Journal .

“The president asked that a group be put together that was going to ensure exactly what he said, which is that we stay the leaders in superintelligence, and that the interests of the American people are put first,” the Journal cited Clayton as saying.

Despite growing concerns about security risks posed by AI, US President Donald Trump has spurned calls for new regulations. Instead, he has prioritised keeping the US ahead of China and backed a voluntary framework involving outside safety audits and stronger internal controls.
“We have a very big lead, and we’re going to keep our lead, and it’s a very positive thing,” the president said during a meeting with industry executives on Sep 29.
The task force has been named the “Super Intelligence Force,” Trump’s preferred name for AI, and will have 120 days to prepare the report, the report said.
Get insights into businesses across South-east Asia

Separately, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent criticised prominent AI leaders’ warnings about existential risks posed by the technology as alarmist and unhelpful, calling on the industry to police itself and produce solutions.

“It is the people at the labs who have to accept responsibility, and I agree with that,” Bessent said in an Axios interview published on Saturday (Oct 3). “I think the labs have come around to that way of thinking, too”. BLOOMBERG

A NEW White House task force will produce a report assessing risks posed by artificial intelligence and what responsibility the US federal government should have over the technology, the Wall Street Journal reported.

The task force will be led by US director of national intelligence Jay Clayton, who confirmed his role to the paper. The role makes Clayton effectively the Trump administration’s new AI czar, a senior White House official told the Wall Street Journal .

“The president asked that a group be put together that was going to ensure exactly what he said, which is that we stay the leaders in superintelligence, and that the interests of the American people are put first,” the Journal cited Clayton as saying.

Burnham said U.K. and U.S. officials are carrying out a “complex and serious” investigation into how and why five men and three vans were near the perimeter of RAF Fairford, a base that has been used by American bombers striking Iran during this year’s war. Five British men in their 20s were arrested Sunday on suspicion of explosives offenses and planning an act of terror, before being released on bail a day later. Police say they found a quantity of an accelerant – gasoline – in the vans, but no explosives. Burnham did not provide details about what the suspects were planning or why the U.K. thinks Iran was involved. He said he would “update people more in due course.” “There are strong indications that Iran played a part in what happened over the weekend at RAF Fairford, but of course it remains an ongoing, complex, and serious police investigation,” Burnham told the BBC in one of a series of interviews with British broadcasters. “And of course, we are working closely with our colleagues in the United States of America.” Iran has denied involvement in the incident. It has previously said that it considers any base used to attack its territory a legitimate target . The base 100 miles (160 kilometers) west of London has been used by American bombers during decades of conflicts in the Middle East, including this year’s war with Iran. Top U.S. officials have criticized the decision to grant the suspects bail, with President Donald Trump saying “I wouldn’t have done that” and Secretary of State Marco Rubio saying a lot of people were “disturbed” by the move. U.K. officials also say proxies linked to Iran have been behind a string of arsons and other attacks in the U.K. and other countries, many of them targeting the Jewish community and intended to sow fear.
