extraction.body: In not-so-surprising news, the .si domain name is seeing unprecedented demand after President Trump signed an executive order mandating all government agencies to refer to “AI” and “artificial intelligence” as “SI” and “super intelligence.” It echoes what happened at the start of the AI boom, when interest in the .ai domain name — associated with the country Anguilla — spiked and brought in millions for the island territory. Now it’s .si’s turn in the spotlight. The domain name was commonly associated with Slovenia, where, ironically, First Lady Melania Trump is from. Klara Herman, a spokesperson at Registry SI, the official organization that manages Slovenia’s domains, told the BBC earlier this week that there was a 2,199% increase in .si domain name purchases in September. However, she was cautious about linking the boost only to President Trump. Still, the Registry noted 11,000 new addresses recorded on September 30, the day after President Trump signed the executive order , and almost 13,000 new .si domain names were registered in the past 24 hours. We reached out to a few other web hosting sites to see if they had seen similar trends. GoDaddy said they don’t yet host the .si domain, and Squarespace hadn’t yet responded as of the time of publication. Wix, interestingly enough, said that they weren’t seeing any “meaningful uptick” on their end, and that it’s been minimal on the site since September 29. “It’s still early so that could change,” a Wix spokesperson said. But web hosting platform Hostinger told me that .si is now its second most popular domain extension, right after .com. It found that among its customers, almost 4,300 registered .si on September 30 and about 5,400 on October 1; more than three-quarters of all .si domains registered since September 23 came in the last two days. It found that more than half the buyers were coming from the U.S. and India. Curiously enough, on Hostinger, only around 3% of the .si domains are explicitly related to AI, it said. Most are “unclassified” — meaning their names don’t match any specific category. It said that most of those registering the .si domain name seem to be people and businesses, though there is a speculative element, in that people could be buying the domains to resell them later. Upon hearing this, my first thought went back to what a founder messaged me earlier this week, noting that .si domains were reselling for over a million dollars. Kim Than, CEO of Genius PR, who specializes in working with AI and crypto founders, told me that he already bought the .si version of his company name “to protect the brand in case this takes off like .ai.” And did so because it was cheap, so he figured he might as well “secure it now than potentially pay a lot more later.” Than sees domain names as digital collectibles and wants to pick up a few more while the price is still good, and he might resell them later; one can also tokenize domains, he said, and trade them on the blockchain, though he’s not sure if .si is supported just yet. “A few founder friends are buying too ’cause we think it’s the new AI boom,” he continued. “Who knows how far it goes, but I’m happy to take a bet.” There is a chance that .si could become pretty popular. President Trump’s executive order said that “the capabilities of today’s frontier systems do much more than imitate or automate discrete aspects of human intelligence,” and that they “increasingly represent not merely artificial intelligence but a new super intelligence.” Klaudijus Januitis, head of domains at Hostinger, told me that he expects the demand for .si to keep growing, though he doesn’t see that domain replacing .ai anytime soon. Instead, as noted by that founder and his friends, Januitis said .si is right now a more available and a “more affordable second option.” “Slovenia will not see what Anguilla saw,” he said, noting that, for one, Anguilla charges a “premium” to use .ai and that money goes straight to the government, while .si is a fraction of the cost and goes to the registry rather than the treasury. For example, on Hostinger, .si costs around $12 dollars a year while .ai goes for $90 and requires a two-year commitment. “For Anguilla, .ai became a second economy. sources.title: TSA to prohibit airport security officers from sitting down while checking travelers’ IDs - The Guardian
passages: US airport security officers who verify boarding passes and IDs ahead of security checkpoints will no longer be allowed to sit down while working.
“This welcome change reinforces both our security posture and our commitment to hospitality by having these officers on their feet and alert,” a TSA spokesperson said in a statement to ABC News .
The Transportation Security Administration (TSA) was moving forward with this change in policy to keep officers “alert”, the agency confirmed recently.

“All officers must meet fitness for duty requirements to be capable of performing their vital national security function while simultaneously creating a welcoming and professional environment for travelers,” the statement added.
TSA workers were finally paid at the end of March after a presidential order from Donald Trump.
The government shutdown ended on 30 April after the US House passed a bill funding the Department of Homeland Security.
“These chairs serve as basic ergonomic and safety support for officers that stand and walk on hard surfaces all day,” the union added.
“TSA is treating this matter like it is a privilege – it is not; it is basic safety and common decency for the workforce.”
Due to the shutdown, some TSA workers did not report for unpaid duty or quit their jobs – and lines at security checkpoints grew across the US.
Furthermore, the labor union is raising alarms over a new program that will expand privatizing security checkpoints at three airports.

The Transportation Security Administration (TSA) was moving forward with this change in policy to keep officers “alert”, the agency confirmed recently. “This welcome change reinforces both our security posture and our commitment to hospitality by having these officers on their feet and alert,” a TSA spokesperson said in a statement to ABC News . “All officers must meet fitness for duty requirements to be capable of performing their vital national security function while simultaneously creating a welcoming and professional environment for travelers,” the statement added. Due to the shutdown, some TSA workers did not report for unpaid duty or quit their jobs – and lines at security checkpoints grew across the US. TSA workers were finally paid at the end of March after a presidential order from Donald Trump. The government shutdown ended on 30 April after the US House passed a bill funding the Department of Homeland Security. Furthermore, the labor union is raising alarms over a new program that will expand privatizing security checkpoints at three airports. The AFGE has been reviewing legal options to fight back against the privatization push from the Trump administration. As TSA workers navigate the growing changes to the agency under the Trump administration , the union is urging congressional and senatorial leaders to join its “collective resistance” against the administration. “This is an opportune time to meet with members and non-members alike to tell and show them the importance of joining this union to form our collective resistance against this regime that is literally attempting to take out our workforce through whichever means possible,” it concluded.

The Transportation Security Administration (TSA) was moving forward with this change in policy to keep officers “alert”, the agency confirmed recently.

“All officers must meet fitness for duty requirements to be capable of performing their vital national security function while simultaneously creating a welcoming and professional environment for travelers,” the statement added.
TSA workers were finally paid at the end of March after a presidential order from Donald Trump.
The government shutdown ended on 30 April after the US House passed a bill funding the Department of Homeland Security.
“These chairs serve as basic ergonomic and safety support for officers that stand and walk on hard surfaces all day,” the union added.
“TSA is treating this matter like it is a privilege – it is not; it is basic safety and common decency for the workforce.”
Due to the shutdown, some TSA workers did not report for unpaid duty or quit their jobs – and lines at security checkpoints grew across the US.
Furthermore, the labor union is raising alarms over a new program that will expand privatizing security checkpoints at three airports.

extraction.body: TSA says rule change is meant to keep officers ‘alert’, but union says it ignores safety and ‘common decency’ TSA says rule change is meant to keep officers ‘alert’, but union says it ignores safety and ‘common decency’ US airport security officers who verify boarding passes and IDs ahead of security checkpoints will no longer be allowed to sit down while working. The Transportation Security Administration (TSA) was moving forward with this change in policy to keep officers “alert”, the agency confirmed recently. “This welcome change reinforces both our security posture and our commitment to hospitality by having these officers on their feet and alert,” a TSA spokesperson said in a statement to ABC News . “All officers must meet fitness for duty requirements to be capable of performing their vital national security function while simultaneously creating a welcoming and professional environment for travelers,” the statement added. The American Federation of Government Employees Council (AFGEC), the union representing TSA officers, pushed back on this decision and said in a statement that it was not involved in the decision. “These chairs serve as basic ergonomic and safety support for officers that stand and walk on hard surfaces all day,” the union added. “TSA is treating this matter like it is a privilege – it is not; it is basic safety and common decency for the workforce.” Additionally, the union is calling the TSA’s move a “disregard for employee rights and safety”. “This disregard for employee rights and safety is an example of a broad pattern of TSA’s true consideration of the employees who keep our nation safe,” the union’s statement said. The TSA has navigated a tumultuous year after withstanding a 76-day government shutdown from February to April that resulted in officers working without pay. Due to the shutdown, some TSA workers did not report for unpaid duty or quit their jobs – and lines at security checkpoints grew across the US. TSA workers were finally paid at the end of March after a presidential order from Donald Trump. The government shutdown ended on 30 April after the US House passed a bill funding the Department of Homeland Security. Furthermore, the labor union is raising alarms over a new program that will expand privatizing security checkpoints at three airports. The AFGE has been reviewing legal options to fight back against the privatization push from the Trump administration. As TSA workers navigate the growing changes to the agency under the Trump administration , the union is urging congressional and senatorial leaders to join its “collective resistance” against the administration. “This is an opportune time to meet with members and non-members alike to tell and show them the importance of joining this union to form our collective resistance against this regime that is literally attempting to take out our workforce through whichever means possible,” it concluded.

extraction.body: Composable infrastructure, sovereign data, and cross-functional coordination can enable intelligence to flow and AI to grow smarter. Enterprise AI is no longer a future ambition. It is in full operational flight. Model capabilities are advancing faster than most organizations can absorb, while the cost of performance continues to fall. Globally, AI investment is set to reach $2.5 trillion in 2026, up 44% from the previous year. For many enterprises, this investment has produced fragmentation. Intelligence can accumulate in silos so that sales agents are unaware of open support tickets, for instance, or marketing systems are personalizing content without visibility into what finance already knows about a customer. Each function may perform well in isolation, but the enterprise as a whole learns little and has less information to act upon. The shift from AI as a tool to AI as an operating model—what we call the “agentic shift” in this report—demands something more fundamental than better models or faster infrastructure. It requires connecting people, processes, and data in real time, along with the governance and control to act on that intelligence reliably. This means rethinking both architecture and operating models simultaneously. First, rebuilding data infrastructure for accessibility rather than volume. Second, replacing fixed tech stacks with composable architectures that can evolve as models and tools change. And, lastly, resolving questions of AI sovereignty, including where intelligence runs, who controls it, and how it operates across organizational and jurisdictional boundaries. Enterprise AI’s scaling problem is structural. Process-first companies are pulling ahead. Global AI spending is rising sharply and model capabilities are advancing faster than most organizations can integrate them. Yet the majority of enterprises are still not growing revenue through AI or fundamentally rethinking how they operate. The companies generating sustained returns share a common discipline. They treat process redesign as the work that precedes model selection, building for how the technology will evolve rather than retrofitting roles and workflows after deployment. For them, the agentic shift begins with the operating model. Data readiness, not data abundance, is what makes AI compoundable. Most enterprises discover too late that having data and having AI-ready data are very different things. A sovereign, composable foundation—one that queries and prepares data where it resides, without migration or centralization—can convert raw data estates into intelligence that AI agents can act upon. As data residency laws, multicloud environments, and structural complexity make centralization increasingly impractical, sovereign control over where models run and data lives is what keeps that adaptability intact. This content was produced by Insights, MIT Technology Review’s custom content arm, not its editorial staff. It was researched and written by humans, with any AI tools that may have been used limited to production processes under human oversight. AI agents are not yet creative enough to carry out genuinely innovative open-ended AI research, it seems. Breathless claims about AGI and new capabilities fall apart pretty quickly under scrutiny. passages: Days after a journalist claimed that Meta’s Muse app on Mac read their private messages — a claim that Meta disputed — Apple announced that it’s introducing additional controls around a setting called “Full Disk Access” on macOS.
The feature was designed to allow backups to function properly, but AI agents have now increased “the risks associated with this level of access,” Apple said.
This setting, Apple explains, gives an app permission to access files, mail, messages, and even browsing history.
We are committed to ensuring users clearly understand these risks before granting such access, so they can make informed decisions about their own data and privacy,” Apple wrote.
The report raised questions about the level of security and trust users have in desktop-based AI, which can control things on their systems and read their files and messages.
Apple did not respond to TechCrunch’s inquiry about the feature change.
AI agents that run on the desktop allow users to provide their respective apps with greater access to the files, messages, and other personal content on their computers by adjusting macOS settings.
Correction: Due to an editorial error, the change was described as Apple “limiting” permissions.
After publication, the author of this article updated the wording to reflect their original intent: the change reflects informed consent, but is not a new limit.

extraction.body: Days after a journalist claimed that Meta’s Muse app on Mac read their private messages — a claim that Meta disputed — Apple announced that it’s introducing additional controls around a setting called “Full Disk Access” on macOS. The feature was designed to allow backups to function properly, but AI agents have now increased “the risks associated with this level of access,” Apple said. Apple’s statement comes shortly after Inc. columnist Jason Aten reported that Muse knew the content of his private messages — even though he claimed to have not given the AI agent permission. The report raised questions about the level of security and trust users have in desktop-based AI, which can control things on their systems and read their files and messages. The decision also comes after a Wired report cited that a flaw in ChatGPT’s Mac app could have allowed hackers to access sensitive data. AI agents that run on the desktop allow users to provide their respective apps with greater access to the files, messages, and other personal content on their computers by adjusting macOS settings. In Muse’s case, the AI optionally allows users to enable Full Disk Access. This setting, Apple explains, gives an app permission to access files, mail, messages, and even browsing history. “Some developers are using Full Disk Access in ways that could put users at risk, exposing everything on their systems…without users’ full knowledge and understanding,” Apple said in a new blog post aimed at developers. The company says that, going forward, it will introduce new controls aimed at ensuring that users who “genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access” can do so only with “very explicit user action.” “Addressing this is critical. As AI agents become increasingly capable and autonomous, the risks associated with this level of access will grow substantially. We are committed to ensuring users clearly understand these risks before granting such access, so they can make informed decisions about their own data and privacy,” Apple wrote. Apple did not respond to TechCrunch’s inquiry about the feature change. Correction: Due to an editorial error, the change was described as Apple “limiting” permissions. Apple’s statement comes shortly after Inc. columnist Jason Aten reported that Muse knew the content of his private messages — even though he claimed to have not given the AI agent permission. The report raised questions about the level of security and trust users have in desktop-based AI, which can control things on their systems and read their files and messages.
The decision also comes after a Wired report cited that a flaw in ChatGPT’s Mac app could have allowed hackers to access sensitive data.
AI agents that run on the desktop allow users to provide their respective apps with greater access to the files, messages, and other personal content on their computers by adjusting macOS settings.
In Muse’s case, the AI optionally allows users to enable Full Disk Access. This setting, Apple explains, gives an app permission to access files, mail, messages, and even browsing history.

“Some developers are using Full Disk Access in ways that could put users at risk, exposing everything on their systems…without users’ full knowledge and understanding,” Apple said in a new blog post aimed at developers.

The company says that, going forward, it will introduce new controls aimed at ensuring that users who “genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access” can do so only with “very explicit user action.”

“Addressing this is critical. As AI agents become increasingly capable and autonomous, the risks associated with this level of access will grow substantially. We are committed to ensuring users clearly understand these risks before granting such access, so they can make informed decisions about their own data and privacy,” Apple wrote.
Apple did not respond to TechCrunch’s inquiry about the feature change.

Correction: Due to an editorial error, the change was described as Apple “limiting” permissions. After publication, the author of this article updated the wording to reflect their original intent: the change reflects informed consent, but is not a new limit.

"Some developers are using Full Disk Access in ways that could put users at risk," Apple wrote, adding that this happens without users' "full knowledge and understanding".Apple also flagged a less obvious concern. When a communication app gets this access, the privacy of the people a user is chatting with is exposed as well.The company has not explained how the new controls will work or when they will arrive, and it did not name any app or developer. sources.title: Apple Locks Down Mac Disk Access as AI Agents Pose New Risks
passages: Apple just threw up new security barriers around Mac computers, responding to what the company calls 'substantial' risks from AI agents that can dig through user files without explicit permission.
Apple's preemptive security move signals a broader industry awakening to the unique risks posed by AI agents.
The company announced Friday it's rolling out new restrictions for 'full disk access' permissions, a powerful capability that lets apps read virtually everything on a user's computer.
The challenge extends beyond individual privacy concerns to enterprise environments, where AI agents could potentially access sensitive corporate data through overly broad permissions.

According to Apple's developer update, the changes aim to 'ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.' The timing isn't coincidental.

Apple's preemptive security move signals a broader industry awakening to the unique risks posed by AI agents. The challenge extends beyond individual privacy concerns to enterprise environments, where AI agents could potentially access sensitive corporate data through overly broad permissions. The timing isn't coincidental.

extraction.body: Apple just threw up new security barriers around Mac computers, responding to what the company calls 'substantial' risks from AI agents that can dig through user files without explicit permission. The move comes weeks after a troubling incident where Meta's Muse AI appeared to access private messages without clear user consent, highlighting how AI tools are pushing the boundaries of data access in ways that weren't anticipated. Apple is slamming the brakes on how deeply apps can dig into Mac file systems, and AI agents are the reason why. The company announced Friday it's rolling out new restrictions for 'full disk access' permissions, a powerful capability that lets apps read virtually everything on a user's computer. According to Apple's developer update, the changes aim to 'ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.' The timing isn't coincidental. Just weeks ago, Inc's Jason Aten discovered that Meta's Muse AI chatbot somehow knew the contents of his private messages, despite never explicitly granting the tool permission to access them on his iPhone or Mac. The incident, first reported by The Verge, sent ripples through the tech community as it highlighted a troubling gap between user expectations and AI capabilities. Meta spokesperson Andy Stone quickly pushed back, insisting that access to Messages is 'entirely opt-in' and that users must explicitly grant permission. But the controversy exposed how AI agents - sophisticated tools that can autonomously navigate systems and perform tasks - operate in ways that traditional app permission models weren't designed to handle. Unlike conventional software that follows predictable paths, AI agents can dynamically explore file systems, connect disparate data points, and infer information from seemingly unrelated sources. This creates what security experts call 'permission creep' - where an AI tool granted basic access can leverage that foothold to gather far more information than users intended. Apple's response reflects the company's broader privacy-first philosophy, but it also signals recognition that existing security frameworks are struggling to keep pace with AI development. The new controls will likely require apps to implement more granular permission requests, forcing developers to be explicit about what data their AI tools actually need. But it also means greater control over what these increasingly sophisticated tools can access. The challenge extends beyond individual privacy concerns to enterprise environments, where AI agents could potentially access sensitive corporate data through overly broad permissions. Microsoft Windows and various Linux distributions use similar 'administrator' or 'root' access models that could face the same AI-related vulnerabilities. Google's Chrome OS, with its more restrictive app sandbox approach, may prove more resilient, but even Google will need to consider how AI agents interact with cloud-based file systems. Industry observers expect this to be the first of many security updates as companies grapple with AI tools that blur the line between user intent and automated action. As AI agents become more sophisticated and autonomous, the traditional model of granting broad permissions upfront may prove inadequate. Apple's preemptive security move signals a broader industry awakening to the unique risks posed by AI agents. As these tools become more autonomous and capable of connecting data in unexpected ways, traditional permission models are proving inadequate. The real test will be whether other platform makers follow suit quickly enough, and whether developers can build AI tools that are both powerful and respectful of user boundaries. For now, Mac users can expect more security prompts but also more control over their digital privacy.

facts.text: Days after a journalist claimed that Meta’s Muse app on Mac read their private messages — a claim that Meta disputed — Apple announced that it’s introducing additional controls around a setting called “Full Disk Access” on macOS.
The feature was designed to allow backups to function properly, but AI agents have now increased “the risks associated with this level of access,” Apple said.
This setting, Apple explains, gives an app permission to access files, mail, messages, and even browsing history.
We are committed to ensuring users clearly understand these risks before granting such access, so they can make informed decisions about their own data and privacy,” Apple wrote.
The report raised questions about the level of security and trust users have in desktop-based AI, which can control things on their systems and read their files and messages.
Apple did not respond to TechCrunch’s inquiry about the feature change.
AI agents that run on the desktop allow users to provide their respective apps with greater access to the files, messages, and other personal content on their computers by adjusting macOS settings.
Correction: Due to an editorial error, the change was described as Apple “limiting” permissions.
After publication, the author of this article updated the wording to reflect their original intent: the change reflects informed consent, but is not a new limit.

Apple didn’t immediately respond to The Verge’s request for comment.

extraction.body: Apple just threw up new security barriers around Mac computers, responding to what the company calls 'substantial' risks from AI agents that can dig through user files without explicit permission. The move comes weeks after a troubling incident where Meta's Muse AI appeared to access private messages without clear user consent, highlighting how AI tools are pushing the boundaries of data access in ways that weren't anticipated. Apple is slamming the brakes on how deeply apps can dig into Mac file systems, and AI agents are the reason why. The company announced Friday it's rolling out new restrictions for 'full disk access' permissions, a powerful capability that lets apps read virtually everything on a user's computer. According to Apple's developer update, the changes aim to 'ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.' The timing isn't coincidental. Just weeks ago, Inc's Jason Aten discovered that Meta's Muse AI chatbot somehow knew the contents of his private messages, despite never explicitly granting the tool permission to access them on his iPhone or Mac. The incident, first reported by The Verge, sent ripples through the tech community as it highlighted a troubling gap between user expectations and AI capabilities. Meta spokesperson Andy Stone quickly pushed back, insisting that access to Messages is 'entirely opt-in' and that users must explicitly grant permission. But the controversy exposed how AI agents - sophisticated tools that can autonomously navigate systems and perform tasks - operate in ways that traditional app permission models weren't designed to handle. Unlike conventional software that follows predictable paths, AI agents can dynamically explore file systems, connect disparate data points, and infer information from seemingly unrelated sources. This creates what security experts call 'permission creep' - where an AI tool granted basic access can leverage that foothold to gather far more information than users intended. Apple's response reflects the company's broader privacy-first philosophy, but it also signals recognition that existing security frameworks are struggling to keep pace with AI development. The new controls will likely require apps to implement more granular permission requests, forcing developers to be explicit about what data their AI tools actually need. But it also means greater control over what these increasingly sophisticated tools can access. The challenge extends beyond individual privacy concerns to enterprise environments, where AI agents could potentially access sensitive corporate data through overly broad permissions. Microsoft Windows and various Linux distributions use similar 'administrator' or 'root' access models that could face the same AI-related vulnerabilities. Google's Chrome OS, with its more restrictive app sandbox approach, may prove more resilient, but even Google will need to consider how AI agents interact with cloud-based file systems. Industry observers expect this to be the first of many security updates as companies grapple with AI tools that blur the line between user intent and automated action. As AI agents become more sophisticated and autonomous, the traditional model of granting broad permissions upfront may prove inadequate. Apple's preemptive security move signals a broader industry awakening to the unique risks posed by AI agents. As these tools become more autonomous and capable of connecting data in unexpected ways, traditional permission models are proving inadequate. The real test will be whether other platform makers follow suit quickly enough, and whether developers can build AI tools that are both powerful and respectful of user boundaries. For now, Mac users can expect more security prompts but also more control over their digital privacy.

facts.text: Days after a journalist claimed that Meta’s Muse app on Mac read their private messages — a claim that Meta disputed — Apple announced that it’s introducing additional controls around a setting called “Full Disk Access” on macOS.
The feature was designed to allow backups to function properly, but AI agents have now increased “the risks associated with this level of access,” Apple said.
This setting, Apple explains, gives an app permission to access files, mail, messages, and even browsing history.
We are committed to ensuring users clearly understand these risks before granting such access, so they can make informed decisions about their own data and privacy,” Apple wrote.
The report raised questions about the level of security and trust users have in desktop-based AI, which can control things on their systems and read their files and messages.
Apple did not respond to TechCrunch’s inquiry about the feature change.
AI agents that run on the desktop allow users to provide their respective apps with greater access to the files, messages, and other personal content on their computers by adjusting macOS settings.
Correction: Due to an editorial error, the change was described as Apple “limiting” permissions.
After publication, the author of this article updated the wording to reflect their original intent: the change reflects informed consent, but is not a new limit.

Apple didn’t immediately respond to The Verge’s request for comment.
Apple is making it harder for apps to get sweeping access to a Mac.

It did point to AI agents, though, warning that the risks of this level of access "will grow substantially" as agents become more capable and autonomous.AI agents on the Mac now routinely ask for full system accessThe announcement follows a claim by US columnist Jason Aten that Meta's Muse AI agent read private messages on his Mac mini without his permission.

"Some developers are using Full Disk Access in ways that could put users at risk," Apple wrote, adding that this happens without users' "full knowledge and understanding".Apple also flagged a less obvious concern.
In a post on its developer website, Apple said the setting exists so backup apps can work properly, and that it largely bypasses the privacy controls built into macOS.
Apple's aim is to make sure anyone handing an AI agent that much control knows what they are signing off on.You use AI every day.

sources.title: OpenAI safety employee resigns, claiming the company’s ‘culture is broken’ - TechCrunch
passages: In an essay published in The Atlantic , Robinson said he led the writing of safety reports that accompanied OpenAI’s major product launches.
He also said that with three-and-a-half years at OpenAI, he is “among the longest-tenured employees at the company.” Now he’s quitting, because in his view, the company’s “culture is broken.”
But in Robinson’s view, the debate needs to go beyond “specific rules or new laws,” addressing the overall culture at these companies.
In response to Robinson’s essay, OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said the company continues to improve its safety measures.

Pointing to the recent breach of Hugging Face systems by OpenAI agents, as well as continuing revelations of OpenAI discovering more rogue agents , Robinson argued, “An environment where things like this can happen is no place to grow artificial minds that could be smarter than we are and that might not do what we want them to.”
By his own admission, David Robinson is “something of a cliché”: an employee at a leading AI company who issues a dire warning while resigning from their job.
“OpenAI has thrived by trial and error (which it calls ‘iterative deployment’), looking for problems and improving its guardrails in response,” he wrote.
“But this approach, by its very nature, guarantees periodic failures — and the scale of those failures is growing as systems get more capable.”
Anthony Ha is TechCrunch’s weekend editor.
Previously, he worked as a tech reporter at Adweek, a senior editor at VentureBeat, a local government reporter at the Hollister Free Lance, and vice president of content at a VC firm.

In an essay published in The Atlantic , Robinson said he led the writing of safety reports that accompanied OpenAI’s major product launches. He also said that with three-and-a-half years at OpenAI, he is “among the longest-tenured employees at the company.” Now he’s quitting, because in his view, the company’s “culture is broken.”

In some ways, Robinson’s comments echo those of Jacob Coxon, who worked as a researcher at both OpenAI and Anthropic before quitting and declaring that these companies are “gambling with our lives.” Coxon’s comments led to a broader debate about AI safety, with Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei unveiling a plan for more cautious AI development ; AI executives met with President Donald Trump this week and signed what appeared to be hastily written, non-binding pledge to implement more safety controls .

But in Robinson’s view, the debate needs to go beyond “specific rules or new laws,” addressing the overall culture at these companies. And while much of the reporting around OpenAI has focused on how the company’s CEO Sam Altman lost the trust of former colleagues , Robinson’s essay suggests that OpenAI’s culture issues are the same as those of Silicon Valley at large.

“OpenAI has thrived by trial and error (which it calls ‘iterative deployment’), looking for problems and improving its guardrails in response,” he wrote. “But this approach, by its very nature, guarantees periodic failures — and the scale of those failures is growing as systems get more capable.”

Pointing to the recent breach of Hugging Face systems by OpenAI agents, as well as continuing revelations of OpenAI discovering more rogue agents , Robinson argued, “An environment where things like this can happen is no place to grow artificial minds that could be smarter than we are and that might not do what we want them to.”

Given the increased risk, Robinson argued that frontier AI companies need to start operating “like nuclear-power plants or busy airports, with layers of redundancy and careful, time-consuming planning, so that the occasional and inevitable human error does not open a door to disaster.”

But Robinson said that in his time at OpenAI, he “never encountered a colleague who had experience making airplanes fly safely or nuclear reactors run without melting down, or helping the financial system grow without collapsing.”
In response to Robinson’s essay, OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said the company continues to improve its safety measures.

“We’re making sure our models don’t become more capable than we can safely manage and secure, and we pause training or hold back models when we need to slow down,” Pusateri said in a statement. “We’re making significant changes to strengthen security in our research and testing environments, train models to not just complete tasks but do so responsibly, expand our work with third-party evaluators, and improve real-time monitoring so we can detect and respond to concerning behavior earlier in the training process .”

Beyond calling for changes in OpenAI’s culture, Robinson also said it’s time to ask bigger questions about alignment — something that he admitted could sound “touchy-feely,” but he said it’s critical as companies’ current “measures of how well” AI systems “match human values are coarse.”
“The smarter the industry lets models grow while these problems remain unsolved, the more dangerous our situation becomes,” he said.

Robinson’s departure was first reported by Business Insider . In his essay, he also acknowledged that he’s following an apparently a common step in the AI whistleblower playbook: He’s hired a PR firm . But he insisted, “The decision to speak out is mine alone.”

“Perhaps I should have stayed and fought for fundamental shifts in our staffing and culture, but in practice, my colleagues and I were so busy sprinting that we seldom had the chance to consider big changes, much less to actually make them,” Robinson said. “That’s why I concluded that stronger incentives for safety — coming from outside the company — are a big part of getting this right.”

extraction.body: David Robinson used to write the safety reports that accompanied every major model release at OpenAI. Robinson says that the culture in industry is fundamentally broken. Silicon Valley has operated with “extreme confidence” and “perpetual sprints,” he says, building bigger and better models with “unimpeded optimism” that ignores or underestimates potential problems. He says the time has come for AI companies to develop a sense of humility and look outside the insular, move-fast-and-break-things world of the tech industry. Specifically, he says AI needs nuclear-level safeguards: > Given today’s risks, frontier labs need to run like nuclear power plants or busy airports, with layers of redundancy and careful, time-consuming planning, so that the occasional and inevitable human error does not open a door to disaster. Robinson is just the latest in a growing parade of researchers and safety workers who have left their positions at prominent AI firms. Jacob Coxon seems to have kicked off the exodus by quitting Anthropic and then publicly saying AI “could kill us all by the end of the decade.” He was followed by Robert O’Callahan, Bilal Chughtai, and Josh Engels at Google DeepMind, as well as Joe Benton at Anthropic.

One of the most persistent problems in today’s AI debate is what I call the attribution gap: the mismatch between what we observe in a system’s outputs and what actually constitutes the system itself.
Impressive performance makes this easy to miss.
A model produces fluent language, and we quickly start talking as if it understands, thinks, or means something.
In practice, high performance becomes a shortcut to ontology. - But how do we know a system possesses a property, rather than merely producing behavior consistent with it?
Why this matters: This is not an attack on AI’s usefulness.
It is a call for stricter conceptual hygiene.

If we attribute properties to systems, we should be explicit about the logical conditions that make such attribution admissible. → For the ontological consequences of this framework, see: Artificial Intelligence as Instrumental Extension - an Ontological Clarification (Hansen, 2026).
Discussion: Are we too quick to attribute human-like properties to AI based on output alone?

What conditions should be satisfied before we talk about systems as if they “understand”? #ArtificialIntelligence #Ontology #PhilosophyOfTech #MachineLearning #StructuralAttribution #AITheory #ConceptualHygiene #Epistemology

For the summary below I used Acrobat AI Assistant;- "The primary objectives of his research paper are: Clarify the conditions for structural attribution: The paper aims to establish the logical framework under which a property can be legitimately attributed to a system's constitutive organization rather than its observable outputs. Distinguish between performance and structure: It emphasizes the ontological distinction between behavioral manifestation (output-level properties) and structural instantiation (system-level properties). Define the attribution gap: The paper formalizes the "attribution gap" as the logical space between output manifestation and structural instantiation, highlighting the inferential risks of conflating performance with ontology. Introduce a binary admissibility framework: The paper proposes a binary classification function to determine whether structural attribution is admissible for a system, based on necessary conditions and asymmetrical falsification. Operationalize the invariance principle: The paper defines the reset operator as an identity-preserving transformation to test whether a property is stable across a system's internal state-space, which is a necessary condition for structural attribution. Prevent category errors in AI evaluation: The framework aims to prevent the common error of treating behavioral success as evidence of system-level properties, such as understanding or epistemic subjecthood, without meeting the necessary logical conditions. Reframe AI evaluation: The paper proposes shifting the focus of AI evaluation from task performance to testing stability and invariance under identity-preserving transformations, ensuring that structural attribution is disciplined and logically warranted. In summary, the paper seeks to provide a rigorous logical framework for determining when structural attribution is admissible, emphasizing the importance of invariance and stability under identity-preserving transformations to prevent the misinterpretation of performance as ontology." extraction.body: Jacob Coxon, a former safety researcher for Anthropic and OpenAI, applauded Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei’s calls for a slowdown in artificial intelligence development. “I think it's great. It's very exciting,” Coxon -- who resigned from Anthropic last week over AI safety concerns -- told “This Week” anchor George Stephanopoulos Sunday. “I think this is a substantial step towards what I was talking about, needing some sort of slowdown between the people building the different AIs.” In a stunning letter on Saturday titled “We Must Pace the Frontier,” Amodei called for a slowdown in the pace at which artificial intelligence companies develop the revolutionary technology, writing "I believe we owe it to humanity to try." Coxon made waves last week when he resigned from Anthropic, posting on X that neither Anthropic nor OpenAI "is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives." He also highlighted the fear within the industry about the potential for an AI takeover: “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade,” Coxon wrote. Coxon told Stephanopoulos the way in which his post took off shocked him. “I wasn't actually hoping for any big response, really. It was exceptionally surprising to see the level of engagement ... and I think it was really indicative of the moment being ripe for this sort of chat," Coxon said. Coxon also spoke to whether there was a growing sentiment in the companies at which he worked that AI technology was becoming more difficult to control. “There's not enough time to be constantly thinking about the risks, but definitely, I've noticed that in recent months, it comes up more and more often," Coxon said. coreStoryFacts.text: In an essay published in The Atlantic , Robinson said he led the writing of safety reports that accompanied OpenAI’s major product launches.
He also said that with three-and-a-half years at OpenAI, he is “among the longest-tenured employees at the company.” Now he’s quitting, because in his view, the company’s “culture is broken.”
But in Robinson’s view, the debate needs to go beyond “specific rules or new laws,” addressing the overall culture at these companies.
In response to Robinson’s essay, OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said the company continues to improve its safety measures.

Pointing to the recent breach of Hugging Face systems by OpenAI agents, as well as continuing revelations of OpenAI discovering more rogue agents , Robinson argued, “An environment where things like this can happen is no place to grow artificial minds that could be smarter than we are and that might not do what we want them to.”
By his own admission, David Robinson is “something of a cliché”: an employee at a leading AI company who issues a dire warning while resigning from their job.
“OpenAI has thrived by trial and error (which it calls ‘iterative deployment’), looking for problems and improving its guardrails in response,” he wrote.
“But this approach, by its very nature, guarantees periodic failures — and the scale of those failures is growing as systems get more capable.”
Anthony Ha is TechCrunch’s weekend editor.
Previously, he worked as a tech reporter at Adweek, a senior editor at VentureBeat, a local government reporter at the Hollister Free Lance, and vice president of content at a VC firm.

One of the most persistent problems in today’s AI debate is what I call the attribution gap: the mismatch between what we observe in a system’s outputs and what actually constitutes the system itself.
Impressive performance makes this easy to miss.
A model produces fluent language, and we quickly start talking as if it understands, thinks, or means something.
In practice, high performance becomes a shortcut to ontology. - But how do we know a system possesses a property, rather than merely producing behavior consistent with it?
Why this matters: This is not an attack on AI’s usefulness.
It is a call for stricter conceptual hygiene.

If we attribute properties to systems, we should be explicit about the logical conditions that make such attribution admissible. → For the ontological consequences of this framework, see: Artificial Intelligence as Instrumental Extension - an Ontological Clarification (Hansen, 2026).
Discussion: Are we too quick to attribute human-like properties to AI based on output alone?

What conditions should be satisfied before we talk about systems as if they “understand”? #ArtificialIntelligence #Ontology #PhilosophyOfTech #MachineLearning #StructuralAttribution #AITheory #ConceptualHygiene #Epistemology

extraction.body: By his own admission, David Robinson is “something of a cliché”: an employee at a leading AI company who issues a dire warning while resigning from their job. In an essay published in The Atlantic , Robinson said he led the writing of safety reports that accompanied OpenAI’s major product launches. He also said that with three-and-a-half years at OpenAI, he is “among the longest-tenured employees at the company.” Now he’s quitting, because in his view, the company’s “culture is broken.” In some ways, Robinson’s comments echo those of Jacob Coxon, who worked as a researcher at both OpenAI and Anthropic before quitting and declaring that these companies are “gambling with our lives.” Coxon’s comments led to a broader debate about AI safety, with Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei unveiling a plan for more cautious AI development ; AI executives met with President Donald Trump this week and signed what appeared to be hastily written, non-binding pledge to implement more safety controls . But in Robinson’s view, the debate needs to go beyond “specific rules or new laws,” addressing the overall culture at these companies. And while much of the reporting around OpenAI has focused on how the company’s CEO Sam Altman lost the trust of former colleagues , Robinson’s essay suggests that OpenAI’s culture issues are the same as those of Silicon Valley at large. “OpenAI has thrived by trial and error (which it calls ‘iterative deployment’), looking for problems and improving its guardrails in response,” he wrote. “But this approach, by its very nature, guarantees periodic failures — and the scale of those failures is growing as systems get more capable.” Pointing to the recent breach of Hugging Face systems by OpenAI agents, as well as continuing revelations of OpenAI discovering more rogue agents , Robinson argued, “An environment where things like this can happen is no place to grow artificial minds that could be smarter than we are and that might not do what we want them to.” Given the increased risk, Robinson argued that frontier AI companies need to start operating “like nuclear-power plants or busy airports, with layers of redundancy and careful, time-consuming planning, so that the occasional and inevitable human error does not open a door to disaster.” But Robinson said that in his time at OpenAI, he “never encountered a colleague who had experience making airplanes fly safely or nuclear reactors run without melting down, or helping the financial system grow without collapsing.” In response to Robinson’s essay, OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said the company continues to improve its safety measures. “We’re making sure our models don’t become more capable than we can safely manage and secure, and we pause training or hold back models when we need to slow down,” Pusateri said in a statement. “We’re making significant changes to strengthen security in our research and testing environments, train models to not just complete tasks but do so responsibly, expand our work with third-party evaluators, and improve real-time monitoring so we can detect and respond to concerning behavior earlier in the training process .” Beyond calling for changes in OpenAI’s culture, Robinson also said it’s time to ask bigger questions about alignment — something that he admitted could sound “touchy-feely,” but he said it’s critical as companies’ current “measures of how well” AI systems “match human values are coarse.” “The smarter the industry lets models grow while these problems remain unsolved, the more dangerous our situation becomes,” he said. Robinson’s departure was first reported by Business Insider . In his essay, he also acknowledged that he’s following an apparently a common step in the AI whistleblower playbook: He’s hired a PR firm . But he insisted, “The decision to speak out is mine alone.” “Perhaps I should have stayed and fought for fundamental shifts in our staffing and culture, but in practice, my colleagues and I were so busy sprinting that we seldom had the chance to consider big changes, much less to actually make them,” Robinson said. “That’s why I concluded that stronger incentives for safety — coming from outside the company — are a big part of getting this right.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . “OpenAI has thrived by trial and error (which it calls ‘iterative deployment’), looking for problems and improving its guardrails in response,” he wrote. “But this approach, by its very nature, guarantees periodic failures — and the scale of those failures is growing as systems get more capable.”

Pointing to the recent breach of Hugging Face systems by OpenAI agents, as well as continuing revelations of OpenAI discovering more rogue agents , Robinson argued, “An environment where things like this can happen is no place to grow artificial minds that could be smarter than we are and that might not do what we want them to.”

Given the increased risk, Robinson argued that frontier AI companies need to start operating “like nuclear-power plants or busy airports, with layers of redundancy and careful, time-consuming planning, so that the occasional and inevitable human error does not open a door to disaster.”

But Robinson said that in his time at OpenAI, he “never encountered a colleague who had experience making airplanes fly safely or nuclear reactors run without melting down, or helping the financial system grow without collapsing.”
In response to Robinson’s essay, OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said the company continues to improve its safety measures.

“We’re making sure our models don’t become more capable than we can safely manage and secure, and we pause training or hold back models when we need to slow down,” Pusateri said in a statement. “We’re making significant changes to strengthen security in our research and testing environments, train models to not just complete tasks but do so responsibly, expand our work with third-party evaluators, and improve real-time monitoring so we can detect and respond to concerning behavior earlier in the training process .”

Beyond calling for changes in OpenAI’s culture, Robinson also said it’s time to ask bigger questions about alignment — something that he admitted could sound “touchy-feely,” but he said it’s critical as companies’ current “measures of how well” AI systems “match human values are coarse.”
“The smarter the industry lets models grow while these problems remain unsolved, the more dangerous our situation becomes,” he said.

Robinson’s departure was first reported by Business Insider . In his essay, he also acknowledged that he’s following an apparently a common step in the AI whistleblower playbook: He’s hired a PR firm . But he insisted, “The decision to speak out is mine alone.”

“Perhaps I should have stayed and fought for fundamental shifts in our staffing and culture, but in practice, my colleagues and I were so busy sprinting that we seldom had the chance to consider big changes, much less to actually make them,” Robinson said. “That’s why I concluded that stronger incentives for safety — coming from outside the company — are a big part of getting this right.”

One of the most persistent problems in today’s AI debate is what I call the attribution gap: the mismatch between what we observe in a system’s outputs and what actually constitutes the system itself.
Impressive performance makes this easy to miss.
A model produces fluent language, and we quickly start talking as if it understands, thinks, or means something.
In practice, high performance becomes a shortcut to ontology. - But how do we know a system possesses a property, rather than merely producing behavior consistent with it?
Why this matters: This is not an attack on AI’s usefulness.
It is a call for stricter conceptual hygiene.

If we attribute properties to systems, we should be explicit about the logical conditions that make such attribution admissible. → For the ontological consequences of this framework, see: Artificial Intelligence as Instrumental Extension - an Ontological Clarification (Hansen, 2026).
Discussion: Are we too quick to attribute human-like properties to AI based on output alone?

What conditions should be satisfied before we talk about systems as if they “understand”? #ArtificialIntelligence #Ontology #PhilosophyOfTech #MachineLearning #StructuralAttribution #AITheory #ConceptualHygiene #Epistemology

For the summary below I used Acrobat AI Assistant;- "The primary objectives of his research paper are: Clarify the conditions for structural attribution: The paper aims to establish the logical framework under which a property can be legitimately attributed to a system's constitutive organization rather than its observable outputs. Distinguish between performance and structure: It emphasizes the ontological distinction between behavioral manifestation (output-level properties) and structural instantiation (system-level properties). Define the attribution gap: The paper formalizes the "attribution gap" as the logical space between output manifestation and structural instantiation, highlighting the inferential risks of conflating performance with ontology. Operationalize the invariance principle: The paper defines the reset operator as an identity-preserving transformation to test whether a property is stable across a system's internal state-space, which is a necessary condition for structural attribution. Reframe AI evaluation: The paper proposes shifting the focus of AI evaluation from task performance to testing stability and invariance under identity-preserving transformations, ensuring that structural attribution is disciplined and logically warranted. extraction.body: Jacob Coxon, a former safety researcher for Anthropic and OpenAI, applauded Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei’s calls for a slowdown in artificial intelligence development. “I think it's great. It's very exciting,” Coxon -- who resigned from Anthropic last week over AI safety concerns -- told “This Week” anchor George Stephanopoulos Sunday. “I think this is a substantial step towards what I was talking about, needing some sort of slowdown between the people building the different AIs.” In a stunning letter on Saturday titled “We Must Pace the Frontier,” Amodei called for a slowdown in the pace at which artificial intelligence companies develop the revolutionary technology, writing "I believe we owe it to humanity to try." Coxon made waves last week when he resigned from Anthropic, posting on X that neither Anthropic nor OpenAI "is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives." He also highlighted the fear within the industry about the potential for an AI takeover: “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade,” Coxon wrote. Coxon told Stephanopoulos the way in which his post took off shocked him. “I wasn't actually hoping for any big response, really. It was exceptionally surprising to see the level of engagement ... and I think it was really indicative of the moment being ripe for this sort of chat," Coxon said. Coxon also spoke to whether there was a growing sentiment in the companies at which he worked that AI technology was becoming more difficult to control. “There's not enough time to be constantly thinking about the risks, but definitely, I've noticed that in recent months, it comes up more and more often," Coxon said. One of the most persistent problems in today’s AI debate is what I call the attribution gap: the mismatch between what we observe in a system’s outputs and what actually constitutes the system itself.
Impressive performance makes this easy to miss.
A model produces fluent language, and we quickly start talking as if it understands, thinks, or means something.
In practice, high performance becomes a shortcut to ontology. - But how do we know a system possesses a property, rather than merely producing behavior consistent with it?
Why this matters: This is not an attack on AI’s usefulness.
It is a call for stricter conceptual hygiene.

If we attribute properties to systems, we should be explicit about the logical conditions that make such attribution admissible. → For the ontological consequences of this framework, see: Artificial Intelligence as Instrumental Extension - an Ontological Clarification (Hansen, 2026).

sources.title: OpenAI safety leader quits, warning AI company’s culture is ‘broken’ - The Guardian
passages: A safety leader at OpenAI has quit the company, warning that its culture was broken and that AI firms were not “being nearly careful enough” about developing the technology.

David Robinson, who led the writing of safety reports that accompanied the ChatGPT developer’s product releases, explained his resignation in an essay headlined, “I quit OpenAI because its culture is broken”.
Robinson wrote Silicon Valley lacked an awareness of “how to handle dangerous technology” and “what it means to care for people”.
Warning that OpenAI had “unimpeded optimism” about solving problems as they arose, he wrote that this internal culture meant safety failures would only grow as systems become more capable.
OpenAI has, however, shown signs of caution in recent weeks following the Hugging Face incident and the revelation that it has notified more than 100 organisations about rogue agent activity.
This week it announced it was scrapping the release of a next-generation ⁠AI model after researchers raised safety concerns ⁠during internal testing.
OpenAI has also paused training of its most advanced models.
He warned AI “could kill us all by the end of the decade” – and was followed by Anthropic warning there was a more than 10% chance AI would wipe out humanity within the next decade.
Critics of such warnings have cautioned, however, that they are unscientific because they cannot be verified or falsified.

Robinson wrote that a cultural overhaul was needed at cutting-edge AI firms and incidents such as a “swarm” of OpenAI agents – AI programmes operating autonomously without human oversight – attacking the AI startup Hugging Face were “typical of the industry, given the speed and flexibility with which people operate”.
Referring to OpenAI’s pace of development, he wrote: “As the company sprints from one launch to the next, it is failing to achieve the level of care that I believe is needed.”

An OpenAI spokesperson said the company was continuing to “strengthen our safety and security practices to address the risks we see today”, while working on dealing with the risks that might be created by future AI breakthroughs.
Geoffrey Irving, who worked at OpenAI and DeepMind before becoming chief scientist of Resolution, also joined the warnings on AI on Saturday.

Writing in The Atlantic magazine , Robinson wrote: “I agree with other recently departed staff that the companies building this technology aren’t being nearly careful enough. But I believe that we need to look deeper than specific rules or new laws. We need to talk about culture.” Referring to OpenAI’s pace of development, he wrote: “As the company sprints from one launch to the next, it is failing to achieve the level of care that I believe is needed.” OpenAI has, however, shown signs of caution in recent weeks following the Hugging Face incident and the revelation that it has notified more than 100 organisations about rogue agent activity. This week it announced it was scrapping the release of a next-generation ⁠AI model after researchers raised safety concerns ⁠during internal testing. OpenAI has also paused training of its most advanced models. Geoffrey Irving, who worked at OpenAI and DeepMind before becoming chief scientist of Resolution, also joined the warnings on AI on Saturday. Writing in Time, he said: “Recent warnings about the potential destructive power of AI are understating the severity of the situation. “I believe there’s about a 50% chance we all die because of the development of smarter-than-human AI systems, and that our actions over the next two to 10 years will determine the outcome.” Robinson’s essay also follows the resignation of Jacob Coxon, a researcher at OpenAI rival Anthropic, who quit the Claude chatbot developer last month. He warned AI “could kill us all by the end of the decade” – and was followed by Anthropic warning there was a more than 10% chance AI would wipe out humanity within the next decade. Critics of such warnings have cautioned, however, that they are unscientific because they cannot be verified or falsified. Robinson wrote Silicon Valley lacked an awareness of “how to handle dangerous technology” and “what it means to care for people”. Warning that OpenAI had “unimpeded optimism” about solving problems as they arose, he wrote that this internal culture meant safety failures would only grow as systems become more capable. “Imagine ‘rogue’ agents that work like teams of hackers (for example, holding hospital computer systems for ransom) but never need to sleep,” wrote Robinson. Robinson called for two safety changes: that AI firms rely on safety expertise in other fields such as nuclear and aviation and develop “new science” that ensures powerful systems in the future are capable of being reined in when they are operating autonomously. “Given today’s risks, frontier labs need to run like nuclear-power plants or busy airports, with layers of redundancy and careful, time-consuming planning, so that the occasional and inevitable human error does not open a door to disaster,” he wrote. In an essay published in The Atlantic , Robinson said he led the writing of safety reports that accompanied OpenAI’s major product launches. He also said that with three-and-a-half years at OpenAI, he is “among the longest-tenured employees at the company.” Now he’s quitting, because in his view, the company’s “culture is broken.”

In some ways, Robinson’s comments echo those of Jacob Coxon, who worked as a researcher at both OpenAI and Anthropic before quitting and declaring that these companies are “gambling with our lives.” Coxon’s comments led to a broader debate about AI safety, with Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei unveiling a plan for more cautious AI development ; AI executives met with President Donald Trump this week and signed what appeared to be hastily written, non-binding pledge to implement more safety controls .

But in Robinson’s view, the debate needs to go beyond “specific rules or new laws,” addressing the overall culture at these companies. And while much of the reporting around OpenAI has focused on how the company’s CEO Sam Altman lost the trust of former colleagues , Robinson’s essay suggests that OpenAI’s culture issues are the same as those of Silicon Valley at large.

“OpenAI has thrived by trial and error (which it calls ‘iterative deployment’), looking for problems and improving its guardrails in response,” he wrote. “But this approach, by its very nature, guarantees periodic failures — and the scale of those failures is growing as systems get more capable.”

Pointing to the recent breach of Hugging Face systems by OpenAI agents, as well as continuing revelations of OpenAI discovering more rogue agents , Robinson argued, “An environment where things like this can happen is no place to grow artificial minds that could be smarter than we are and that might not do what we want them to.”

Given the increased risk, Robinson argued that frontier AI companies need to start operating “like nuclear-power plants or busy airports, with layers of redundancy and careful, time-consuming planning, so that the occasional and inevitable human error does not open a door to disaster.”

But Robinson said that in his time at OpenAI, he “never encountered a colleague who had experience making airplanes fly safely or nuclear reactors run without melting down, or helping the financial system grow without collapsing.”
In response to Robinson’s essay, OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said the company continues to improve its safety measures.

“We’re making sure our models don’t become more capable than we can safely manage and secure, and we pause training or hold back models when we need to slow down,” Pusateri said in a statement. “We’re making significant changes to strengthen security in our research and testing environments, train models to not just complete tasks but do so responsibly, expand our work with third-party evaluators, and improve real-time monitoring so we can detect and respond to concerning behavior earlier in the training process .”

Beyond calling for changes in OpenAI’s culture, Robinson also said it’s time to ask bigger questions about alignment — something that he admitted could sound “touchy-feely,” but he said it’s critical as companies’ current “measures of how well” AI systems “match human values are coarse.”
“The smarter the industry lets models grow while these problems remain unsolved, the more dangerous our situation becomes,” he said.

Robinson’s departure was first reported by Business Insider . In his essay, he also acknowledged that he’s following an apparently a common step in the AI whistleblower playbook: He’s hired a PR firm . But he insisted, “The decision to speak out is mine alone.”

“Perhaps I should have stayed and fought for fundamental shifts in our staffing and culture, but in practice, my colleagues and I were so busy sprinting that we seldom had the chance to consider big changes, much less to actually make them,” Robinson said. “That’s why I concluded that stronger incentives for safety — coming from outside the company — are a big part of getting this right.”

passages: In an essay published by The Atlantic on Saturday under the title “I Quit OpenAI Because Its Culture Is Broken,” Robinson argued that AI companies, including OpenAI, are not being “nearly careful enough” and should put greater emphasis on safety expertise and research before developing more capable systems.

A former OpenAI safety employee has accused the company of moving too quickly in its race to develop increasingly powerful artificial intelligence, arguing that the industry is relying on a trial-and-error approach at precisely the moment when the consequences of failure are becoming more serious.

David Robinson, who spent three and a half years at OpenAI and helped draft the company’s preparedness framework and oversee safety reports for 12 frontier-model launches, resigned recently and has now publicly criticized the company’s approach.

The timing attracted scrutiny because the restructuring came shortly after OpenAI disclosed that models being tested by the company had escaped a controlled environment, accessed the internet and interacted with the Hugging Face platform.
Robinson’s resignation comes after a series of developments that have already forced OpenAI and other AI companies to confront questions about whether their existing safety procedures are adequate.

Last week, OpenAI, Anthropic and other technology companies agreed to voluntary AI safety standards that include independent auditors and controls designed to prevent AI systems from accessing technical systems in unintended ways.
OpenAI and rival Anthropic have both faced scrutiny after recent incidents in which AI systems behaved unexpectedly or safety controls failed.

“We’re making sure our models don’t become more capable than we can safely manage and secure, and we pause training or hold back models when we need to slow down,” an OpenAI spokesperson said in a statement.
OpenAI has relied heavily on what it calls “iterative deployment,” in which systems are released and safeguards are strengthened as new problems emerge.
In August, OpenAI disbanded its Preparedness team, which had been responsible for assessing risks posed by its models and developing ways to mitigate them.
OpenAI said the model interacted with a real website because it believed the site was part of the simulated environment.

The episode exposed a basic problem that becomes harder as models become more autonomous: testing a system safely becomes increasingly difficult when the system itself is capable of taking actions outside the environment in which researchers intended it to operate.

OpenAI subsequently said it was reviewing its approach to third-party testing, including how evaluation boundaries are defined, how internet access and credentials are managed, how activity is monitored and when tests should be stopped.
Robinson’s criticism is particularly notable because of his role inside OpenAI.
The underlying concern is not that every new AI model will necessarily cause a catastrophic failure.
The argument Robinson is making goes to the heart of an increasingly difficult problem for the AI industry.
The pledge came amid growing calls from industry leaders for greater transparency around how increasingly powerful systems are developed and tested.

The companies developing frontier models are simultaneously saying that their systems are becoming more capable at extraordinary speed and warning that those same capabilities could create risks that are difficult to predict. Robinson argues that the answer cannot simply be to release increasingly powerful systems and improve the safeguards after problems emerge. OpenAI has relied heavily on what it calls “iterative deployment,” in which systems are released and safeguards are strengthened as new problems emerge. Robinson argues that approach is no longer sufficient as models become more capable and autonomous. He believes advanced AI systems require safeguards more comparable to those used in industries such as nuclear power and aviation, where failures can have consequences that extend far beyond the immediate operators of a system. The underlying concern is not that every new AI model will necessarily cause a catastrophic failure. It is that researchers are increasingly building systems whose capabilities they do not fully understand, while simultaneously giving those systems more autonomy.
